text:
Zimbabwe's first lithium sulfate plant, built by China-owned Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe at Goromonzi, reached full operational status in May 2026, mines minister Polite Kambamura confirmed last week. The $400 million facility is Africa's first lithium sulfate plant the first beneficiation announcement in Zimbabwe's sector to convert from construction to verified operating capacity.

Carbonate unit still pre-commercial. PLZ's lithium carbonate refining facility is reported near completion but unconfirmed operational; more sulfate capacity is expected sector-wide ahead of Zimbabwe's full concentrate export ban, effective January 2027.

Policy driver. Zimbabwe froze raw mineral exports in February 2026 ahead of the 2027 ban, forcing producers to build domestic processing capacity or lose export access. The restriction extends to 13 minerals beyond lithium, including cobalt, PGMs, and rare earths, from January 2027.

Investment context. Over $1 billion in lithium sector investment has been logged since February 2026, per policy expert Tedious Ncube though the figure is undisaggregated by project and may blend processing and upstream mining capex.

Battery manufacturing remains aspirational. Kambamura flagged domestic battery and solar panel production as a longer-term goal, with no capex, partner, or timeline attached. South Africa currently leads Africa's nascent battery-manufacturing capacity.

SMM View: Goromonzi is the first verified beneficiation capacity milestone in Zimbabwe's lithium sector log as confirmed, distinct from carbonate and the $1bn aggregate unverified, project-level breakdown pending). Key watch point: whether sulfate or carbonate capacity build keeps pace with the January 2027 export cutoff or risks a supply disruption relevant to our Zimbabwe ban scenario model.

name: EPA
title: Episode 101: States Back Challenge to EPA Power: SCOTUS Push
description:
Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, 20 states is great, and led by West Virginia, which obviously was the – Zhonette Brown: 21 states.
Mark Chenoweth: That’s right, West Virigina plus 20, that’s a good point.
Zhonette Brown: Although here, the scheme was handed to them by Congress, so they’re only very small part to blame.
Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, absolutely.
Mark Chenoweth: Yeah.
text:
Mark Chenoweth: If you think that unwritten law doesn’t affect you, think again. Whether you’re a business owner, a professional, just an average citizen, you are unknowingly going to fall under vague and unofficial rules, and when bureaucrats act like lawmakers, they’re really restricting your liberty without the consent of the governed. Welcome to Unwritten Law with Mark Chenoweth and John Vecchione. We are pleased to be joined by NCLA general counsel Zhonette Brown, who has been spearheading a case at the United States Supreme Court. This is our non-delegation case against the Environmental Protection Agency, Choice Refrigerants v. EPA, and we just had several amicus briefs filed in support of the cert petition at the Supreme Court. Zhonette, so how many briefs were filed, and who filed?

John Vecchione: Thanks, very happy to be here, and I’m happy to say there were seven amicus briefs that were filed in support of the Choice petition. They were filed West Virginia, joined by 20 other states, filed a brief advancing American freedom. Americans for Prosperity Foundation, the Cato Institute, the Manhattan Institute, Southeastern Legal Foundation, and Mountain States Legal Foundation all filed briefs.

Mark Chenoweth: Sounds like a lot of the usual suspects who support these sort of efforts to – on the non-delegation doctrine, but also, sort of, wider efforts to push back against things that government agencies may be doing wrong.

Zhonette Brown: Absolutely.

John Vecchione: Except maybe the states. They sometimes need a little prodding, so that’s quite – I think that many states is a little unusual.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, 20 states is great, and led by West Virginia, which obviously was the –

Zhonette Brown: 21 states.

Mark Chenoweth: Oh, 21 states.

John Vecchione: Oh, there we go.

Mark Chenoweth: That’s right, West Virigina plus 20, that’s a good point. That’s a good point. So, this is more than 40% of the states. What I was gonna say is that obviously, the titular state involved in the West Virginia v. EPA case, with the major questions doctrine, so a state that knows something about this area of the law and is interested in having something to say.

Zhonette Brown: And, EPA’s specific proclivities to overreach.

Mark Chenoweth: Yes, absolutely.

Zhonette Brown: Although here, the scheme was handed to them by Congress, so they’re only very small part to blame.

Mark Chenoweth: [Laughs] Fair enough. So, where would you like to start? Tell me about one of the amicus briefs that you found to be particularly helpful.

Zhonette Brown: Well, since we were just talking about the states, we can start with that one. One of the points the states makes, sort of their main point, is how broad delegations really interfere with the role of the states as laboratories for democracy. When, because of the pre-emption law, when Congress gives a broad delegation to an agency, and the agency then, as they usually do, tries to expand and overreach, that takes more and more power away from the states under federal pre-emption. And so, that was one of the points that West Virginia made. Another point that West –

Mark Chenoweth: Can I stick on that point for one second, ‘cause I thought that was a great point and something that folks don’t necessarily think about when they think about pre-emption. It’s fine for Congress to pass a law that pre-empts a state law, but when Congress is handing something off to an executive agency and the agency does a regulation that then purports to overrule state law, that’s a little different. That’s not squarely within the supremacy clause.

John Vecchione: And in fact, since pre-emption is such a powerful kind of block on federalism in a lot of ways, particularly with the expansion of the Commerce Clause, you do have to monitor the agencies, because as we’ve seen constantly, they want to aggrandize their power. The only actor in the Constitutional structure that doesn’t wanna aggrandize his power, apparently, is Congress. So, the thing is, so this pre-emption power was given to Congress for very good reasons, but to give it to the administrative agencies, which always want more without any kind of block by either the Congress or the courts because of how these delegations have been allowed, is really a prescription for disaster.

Zhonette Brown: Well, and part of West Virginia’s point is the states’ role in Congress, I mean the representatives, the senators, they’re from the states. They have interest in their home jurisdiction. The states’ role in Congress is part of the structural protection built into bicameralism and presentment, because the states are represented, whereas agencies have no allegiance, loyalty, or reporting to states. So, that was a good point, too, about how overbroad delegations hurt states’ interests.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, absolutely. And then, you were saying another point that they made in their brief.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, another point that they made in their brief that I think that is important, and apparently some people debate, is whether or not major questions plays a significant enough role in protecting from non-delegation. And, the states explained why neither getting rid of Chevron nor the major question doctrine provides enough protection for the structural interests the Constitution requires for non-delegation for the separation of powers and the states.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, I thought that was a fantastic point, as well, and I have been surprised at the extent to which people have tried to turn the major questions doctrine into an alternative to some sort of non-delegation doctrine, because it doesn’t purport to do that much. I mean, I look at it as a clear statement principle. Yes, it’s true if Congress hasn’t spoken clearly, that is gonna have an interpretive outcome, okay fine, but if Congress has spoken clearly, you’re not off the Constitutional hook. You’re still not allowed to delegate your legislative power away, so where are we then? We still need to have a non-delegation doctrine.

Zhonette Brown: Right. And then, the last point that I thought the states made that is sort of unique to the states is, “Hey, if you think this is a problem, it’s not. If you think having a robust non-delegation doctrine is a problem, it’s not, and the states can show that to you.”

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, a couple states have one.

Zhonette Brown: Exactly, and they pointed out perhaps the standard that Florida uses might be useful here, etc. So, I thought just having that role – I don’t remember them filing anything like that, for example, in the FCC versus Consumers Research case, so having that new input from the states, I think, is very helpful.

John Vecchione: And, it was hugely helpful in Loper Bright and Relentless when they said, “Look, we’ve done this, and the sky hasn’t fallen.” Hugely helpful.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, I think that’s right. So, who other than the states?

Zhonette Brown: So, the next one that I’ll talk about is Advancing American Freedom. They thought they had an interesting argument. They argued that not only is there the structural, sort of, issue against delegation, but that delegation should be actually not allowed except as it can fit squarely within the Necessary and Proper Clause. So, their argument, basically, is we are a government of enumerated powers. Congress has powers enumerated to it. The power to delegate is not an enumerated power. The power to delegate is therefore [inaudible] [00:07:25] by the Necessary and Proper Clause, and they went through all of the various reasons why delegation of legislative power cannot be either necessary or proper.

Mark Chenoweth: That’s interesting.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, I thought it was an approach that I hadn’t seen before when I was going through, for example, the FCC versus Consumer Research briefs, etc., so –

Mark Chenoweth: It’s novel.

Zhonette Brown: And, they had a number of people signing on to their brief as well. I don’t – it was a lot, so I don’t remember who all.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, that’s sort of their stock in trade, is getting as many other folks to sign on to their amicus briefs.

John Vecchione: Correct, and I’m wondering, because that necessary and proper sounds very much like the Fifth Circuit distillery case that just came out not a few days before we’re taping this, and they made the same type of argument as to what necessary and proper means. And, hopefully, it’s got legs.

Zhonette Brown: Well, something eventually has to work to get this non-delegation doctrine under control.

Mark Chenoweth: [Laughs] That’s right.

Zhonette Brown: Americans for Prosperity Foundation were the first to file an amicus brief. They did way ahead of the deadline, and they really covered, sort of, all of the upsides and downsides. The real problem with what, first of all, the non-delegation is so important, why the separation of powers is so important, the consent of the governed, and I thought they did a good job of pointing out, sort of, all of the problems that arise from the devolution of the non-delegation doctrine about removing government – the action of governing from the people and how that brings too much importance, for example, to the presidential election, causes polarization, causes alienation, and, sort of, all the practical problems that have evolved and shown themselves over time as the non-delegation doctrine has been waning.

Mark Chenoweth: And, that might appeal to the Justices that you may have been – gonna chime in to say the same thing, this came up in oral argument in Relentless and Loper Bright, the justices did seem to be concerned about the ways in which some of these doctrines and cases have had that impact, and they were wanting to take a step back from that.

John Vecchione: I do. I laughed a little when you said that it was filed early, ‘cause I noticed that Michael Pepson wrote it, and he can write these so fast. But one of the things that came up on here was delegation run riot has had awful effects on our constitutional republic. And, just that little caption there, I think, really covers it, because the justices have been saying to Congress, “Do your job. Do your job. Do your job,” and by not policing things through the non-delegation, the Court itself has walked away from that message they’ve been trying to send in just about every other area.

Mark Chenoweth: Well, and I think the particular thing that came up in oral argument in Relentless was this idea that the stakes in a presidential election have gotten to be so huge because all these decisions made at the executive agency level just flip, sometimes 180 degrees, and so that’s just raising the stakes in a way that, if Congress were making the decisions, there would be more stability over time. You wouldn’t have quite as much at stake in these elections, and that would just overall, maybe, turn down the national temperature on political debate a bit. The Court seemed interested in that outcome, or that seemed like a rationale behind what they did in doing away with the Chevron doctrine. I wonder if that same sort of analysis is what Mike Pepson and the Americans for Prosperity Foundation might be trying to bring into the non-delegation debate.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, and they weren’t the only ones who brought up, sort of, the administrative or regulatory whiplash. It’s not just the effect that it has on us as “We the People” and our relationship with government, but it’s the effect that it has, as one of them pointed out, on entities like Choice, which have to suffer this whiplash and not be able to invest, knowing what the next administration’s gonna do to their business when they’re regulated in this way.

Mark Chenoweth: Right. It reminds me of the movie. Have you seen Whiplash, John?

John Vecchione: I have not.

Mark Chenoweth: “Are you rushing or are you dragging?” It’s like the Supreme Court. “Are you rushing or are you dragging?” Okay.

Zhonette Brown: It depends on the day.

Mark Chenoweth: There may be a slap involved in there from J. K. Simmons in that, but anyway.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, and the Cato Institute sort of followed suit on some of those issues, followed up on the regulatory whiplash, etc., but put it in the context, really framed it as a rule of law problem. When the “rule of law” is regulations, they can change the interpretation 180 degrees every 4 years, right, that is a rule of law problem. And also, here, in non-delegation, you have the same organization, EPA, writing the law, enforcing the law, and, in some cases, acting in a judicial capacity, right? And so, that creates the obvious, sort of, rule of law problem that the Founders were trying to prevent.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, absolutely, and I guess none of us have the James Madison coaster here, but we have one at the office that talks about this. If laws are changed so rapidly that no one knows one day what they’re going to be the next day, then liberty suffers. What other amicus briefs were brought to bear here?

Zhonette Brown: A couple of the briefs, in particular Manhattan Institute, Mountain States, and Southeastern Legal, in part focused on how the problem of the statute here was enhanced by what the DC Circuit actually did, because the DC Circuit chose constitutional avoidance, constitutional doubt, whatever you want to call it. They created, basically out of whole cloth, the intelligible principal that was missing, and that creates even worse problems in our already horrible non-delegation doctrine.

John Vecchione: And, that is something that I think the Court should take just based on that, because I think we’ve said it in our main –

Mark Chenoweth: As in disciplining the lower courts?

John Vecchione: The main thing here is that what the DC Circuit seems to be doing is making a rational basis test for the non-delegation doctrine, where the government does not come up with what the words are that cabin its activities, that came from Congress. They don’t come up with it. So, the DC Circuit gets its clerks together and thinks, “Well, what exactly is the intelligible principal here, since the government hasn’t given us one?” and that’s kinda how rational basis worked for many, many years, right, and that’s not helpful.

Mark Chenoweth: It’s not helpful, and I think under the existing doctrine, the intelligible principle has to come from Congress, not from the courts, so –

John Vecchione: That’s exactly right. That’s the problem with it. And, I will just say, I noticed James Dickey was on the Southeastern Legal Foundation, and he had been our local counsel in the Stewart case years ago, and he was moving off to there, and this is the first brief I’ve seen. But, I’m glad he took up that point.

Zhonette Brown: Absolutely. One other thing that Manhattan Institute said is it’s not only the courts, necessarily, that are gonna go hunting for an intelligible principal in other statutes. Now that the court has led the way, the agencies will do it, right, so you won’t have the agencies at a loss so much for an intelligible principle if Congress didn’t supply one, because they’ll go find it in some theoretically like statute. In this case, the statute was 20 years older, had different language, wasn’t incorporated, wasn’t referenced. There’s all sorts of reasons why it should not have applied, but if it’s good enough for the DC Circuit, it’s gonna be good enough for the agencies.

Mark Chenoweth: Well, and that puts us back in deference land. I mean, it’s sort of like –

John Vecchione: It really does.

Mark Chenoweth: – FCC v. City of Arlington, and Chief Justice Roberts was very eloquent in the dissent in that case, saying, “Wait a minute, the agencies can’t be in control of, sort of, the bounds of their own jurisdiction. That’s not a real, sort of –”

John Vecchione: Guess which way their jurisdiction will go if that happens? I’m just gonna lay it out there. I wonder, yeah.

Mark Chenoweth: Talk about your one-way ratchets.

Zhonette Brown: That harms the states.

Mark Chenoweth: Yes, absolutely, absolutely harms the states. And so, yeah, I think that’s a great point. Glad that that’s in the mix, as well.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, and then, the Southeastern Legal Foundation, of course, was talking about the misuse – related to what we were just talking about for the DC Circuit, the misuse of constitutional doubt, how it cannot be the role of the courts to go and find this solution, and doing so is really sort of an abdication of their responsibility to actually rule on the constitutional question. And, citing Justice Kavanagh, before he was on the bench, before he was on the Supreme Court, had written an article sort of addressing non-delegation, bringing that point up. I hope that he remembers.

Mark Chenoweth: Well, it’ll be easier for him. It’s always good to have an amicus brief that refreshes the recollection of the justices about something they wrote when in an academic posture.

John Vecchione: Exactly.

Mark Chenoweth: So, tell me where – well, are there any other ones that you wanted to highlight today?

Zhonette Brown: No, like Southeastern, Mountain States Legal Foundation largely focused on, sort of, the problem with the approach the DC Circuit took, all of the ways in which it was wrong, and then all of the risks that that creates, particularly given that DC is sort of a central clearinghouse for cases against the administrative state. So, the fact that it’s concentrated there and they’re leading the way in this wild, wild effort to avoid non-delegation, is particularly problematic.

Mark Chenoweth: Well, and that underscores something that was in the cert petition itself, which is the message that this sends to petitioners like our client, if courts are able to go and sort of do their own spadework and find an intelligible principle, then why would anybody ever bother to bring a challenge to something on a non-delegation basis? You’re not gonna be able to win if a court’s willing to go and sort of supply the thing that’s missing.

John Vecchione: That’s exactly right. That’s why, when you challenge something on rational basis, you always have a hard row to hoe, don’t you?

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, absolutely.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, and that’s been Manhattan Institute’s point. Basically, if the non-delegation doctrine wasn’t dead, it is now.

Mark Chenoweth: In the DC Circuit, yeah.

Zhonette Brown: If you let this stand, it is now.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, well that –

John Vecchione: And, I’ll just give a shoutout. I saw Ilya Shapiro’s always on those, but Trevor Burrus is back, who was his compatriot over at Cato when he was doing them. So, the band is back together.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, this is a lot of the usual suspects I was saying, although not in the lineup sense, but in the sense of folks who care about this issue, know about this issue, and are all identifying this case as a good vehicle for the Court to jump back in to the non-delegation question. So, I view that as a great sign.

Zhonette Brown: Right, and obviously I sort of skipped over that point, but because it is waiting trying to get a cert granted, a lot of it was, sort of, this AIM Act really is problematic. This AIM Act, it really does have no standard. It’s so much like Schechter and those other cases. If this passes muster, non-delegation is dead, and so – and then, also, it’s a recent law, it hasn’t been largely interpreted, it doesn’t fit major questions, so…

John Vecchione: And, I thought it was important, and because I think these folks do know this, they all did make amicus briefs for a cert petition telling the [inaudible] [00:19:14] court why they should take this and not why this whole thing’s bad. They did say why you have to take this, which is the main goal here.

Mark Chenoweth: Well, and some of our listeners may not know, sort of, the way that this works mechanically behind the scenes, but at the Supreme Court, the cert petition will go to the cert pool, and there may be one or two justices who aren’t participating in the cert pool, but –

John Vecchione: Gorsuch and Alito.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. Most of the justices do, and so whoever is producing the memo out of the cert pool has a choice between, sort of, doing an abbreviated memo and then what they call the long memo. And, if you have this many amicus briefs that are filed in support of a cert petition, it really forces them to do the longer version of the cert memo, and that always gives your case a better chance of having a more robust discussion in conference, of garnering more attention from the justices, makes it harder for the Department of Justice to ignore the case or downplay it, etc. So, I think all those things are – it’s why we love to have amicus briefs in support of cert petitions, and these are strong, substantive amicus briefs that I think are advancing the cause.

Zhonette Brown: Yes. I was very happy to see them come in. I do think that it will enhance the likelihood that we are able to get a cert.

Mark Chenoweth: So, where do things stand now, timewise?

Zhonette Brown: So, now we wait, again, we wait for the government, and there were interveners in this case, the trade association. They have until May 13th to file their response to our petition. So, we will wait for that to come in and see what they say.

Mark Chenoweth: Okay, and once that happens, then we will have an opportunity for a reply brief, a couple weeks, and then it goes to conference for the justices to mull over.

Zhonette Brown: Exactly.

Mark Chenoweth: So, is it our expectation this’ll all be done by the end of June? We’ll know one way or the other if the Court’s gonna hear this case next term?

Zhonette Brown: Right. It’s our expectation by the end of June we’ll know whether they’re gonna hear it, and then, obviously, the substantive briefing would occur over the summer and the early fall, and it would be heard at some point next term.

title: Utah courts Singapore investors for critical minerals | The Straits Times
description:
“We did a trade mission to Japan and Korea almost two years ago and had tremendous success with bringing Utah companies to invest in Asia and vice versa,” Cox said.
Cox had a pitch for Singapore investors who have typically favoured other American states, such as Texas.
Close to 60 Singapore companies currently operate in Texas.
Its director for the Americas Lim Seow Hui told ST that it continues to see “steady interest from Singapore companies looking to establish and deepen their in-market presence in the US”.
Growing critical industries Rio Tinto, one of the largest foreign companies operating in Utah, produces the critical minerals of copper and tellurium at its massive Kennecott mine near the capital.
text:
SALT LAKE CITY, Utah – Home to mountains, deserts and the largest saltwater lake in the western hemisphere, the US state of Utah has increasingly attracted foreign investment, but flows from Asia account for only a sliver of the pie.

Outreach to the region has helped, said Utah Governor Spencer Cox, pointing to the landlocked state’s trade missions to Japan and South Korea, and the launch of a direct flight from its capital of Salt Lake City to Seoul in June 2025.

“We did a trade mission to Japan and Korea almost two years ago and had tremendous success with bringing Utah companies to invest in Asia and vice versa,” Cox said.

“With our Asian friends, it really started in tourism because they started visiting. We had that link to Asia.

“Where we are seeing investment right now is in life sciences, aerospace, defence and energy. Those sectors have been a real positive for us.”

It comes as Utah’s trove of critical minerals, with applications ranging from defence to artificial intelligence, has drawn attention.

The state’s reserves of critical minerals are one of the most diverse in the US, and lawmakers earlier in 20 26 established a long-term drive to meet 20 per cent to 25 per cent of domestic demand.

Cox had a pitch for Singapore investors who have typically favoured other American states, such as Texas. “We’re the Texas of the Mountain West. You get the same type of low regulation, but you also get a lot more attention,” he told The Straits Times during a press tour organised by the US State Department’s Foreign Press Centre.

The state offers businesses incentives such as tax credits for firms that perform and create high-paying jobs.

Close to 60 Singapore companies currently operate in Texas. They are among over 250 Singapore firms present across 45 states in the US, in sectors including logistics, real estate and professional services.

Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG), which helps businesses expand overseas, opened a US office in Texas earlier in 2026 to work alongside its offices in New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco.

Its director for the Americas Lim Seow Hui told ST that it continues to see “steady interest from Singapore companies looking to establish and deepen their in-market presence in the US”.

She added: “Opportunities are increasingly emerging beyond traditional gateways such as New York and San Francisco.”

Foreign investment push

Foreign direct investment (FDI) in the US has grown by more than a trillion US dollars since 2020 to US$5.86 trillion (S$7.5 trillion) in 2025, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The manufacturing industry saw the largest increase in FDI, led by companies producing electrical equipment and components.

Jonathan Samford, president of Global Business Alliance, which supports foreign investors, said US President Donald Trump has been clear about wanting more investment on US soil.

“The welcome extends well beyond Washington. In our latest national survey, 75 per cent of American voters viewed international companies favourably, up from 62 per cent two years ago, and that support runs across both parties,” he said.

A recent report by fDi Intelligence, a subsidiary of the Financial Times, found that Texas, New York and California secured more FDI projects than other US states did, based on deal announcements made from 2020 to 2025.

Utah drew US$4.9 billion in FDI and was placed 32nd in terms of FDI capital expenditure over the period. It recorded US$40.3 billion in investments from other parts of the US.

Still, the report noted: “The state attracted its second-highest capital expenditure pledges in 2025 since records began.

“Japanese investors have been the most active, thanks to Sekisui House’s multiple residential projects. This reflects strong inward migration of new residents from other parts of the US since the Covid-19 pandemic.”

The other top foreign investors in Utah were the United Kingdom, France, Canada and Australia.

There was no indication of the investment that can be attributed to Singapore, although industry sources said the Asian region accounts for a minority of investors in Utah.

Growing critical industries

Rio Tinto, one of the largest foreign companies operating in Utah, produces the critical minerals of copper and tellurium at its massive Kennecott mine near the capital.

Copper is essential for building data centres, power grid infrastructure and electric vehicles, while tellurium, recovered as a by-product of copper refining, is critical in the production of advanced thin-film solar panels.

A spokesperson for the British-Australian firm said the open-pit mine is “strategically important not only for Rio Tinto, but (also) for the United States’ broader efforts to build secure domestic supply chains”.

“Kennecott hosts a world-class copper orebody, a skilled local workforce, strong industrial infrastructure, and a community that understands the importance of responsible mining,” the spokesperson added.

The firm is exploring an expansion of its mine, which will produce some 1.5 million additional tonnes of copper.

Brian Somers, president of the Utah Mining Association, said it is working with existing mining facilities, including Kennecott, to step up critical mineral production, instead of spending years developing new operations in the state.

“We can’t do things the way we’ve done in the past. Unfortunately, China really does have us over a barrel with a lot of these mineral supply chains, so we’ve got to accelerate the time to market,” he said.

Austrian manufacturer Doppelmayr is set to nearly double the size of its Utah production facility in September as part of a US$60 million expansion in the state.

The company builds ropeway systems deployed around the world, including the Singapore Cable Car’s Sentosa line.

Doppelmayr USA chief executive Keith Johns said the firm benefited from more people venturing outdoors in the US and around the world after the pandemic.

Even so, demand for the firm’s products has been affected by tariffs imposed by the Trump administration. It sources components such as haul ropes – steel cables used to move chair lifts and cabins up and down mountains – from outside the US as it cannot find local manufacturers.

Johns said: “Tariffs that are imposed on those. Someone has got to pay them.

“Some of our customers have delayed investments and some have said, we are going forward with it, but tariffs have definitely had an impact.”

What lies ahead

There are hopes that investment in Utah could grow.

Washington-based BGR Analytics in a 2024 index ranked Utah as the top state for Asian investment, considering metrics including economic profile, business climate and strength of workforce.

The state of 3.5 million people is also seeing the fastest growth in its working-age population among US states, which can help to drive economic growth, recent data released by the US Census Bureau showed. The number of 25- to 64-year-olds in Utah jumped by 10.8 per cent between April 1, 2020 and July 1, 2025.

Over the years, officials have also made progress in shedding Utah’s reputation as a “flyover state”, a term often used to describe territories passed over by travellers.

Its ski resorts, drawing swathes of visitors during winter, transform into popular mountain biking trails and concert venues in the summer months.

Cox’s administration in May also launched a “Utah Elevated” plan to drive economic development through 2035, which includes targeting foreign and domestic investments. Among other priorities, it will tap Utah’s position as host of the 2034 Winter Olympics to drive infrastructure investments.

David Carlebach, chief operating officer and managing director for World Trade Center Utah, which works with the state to attract investment, said: “The biggest challenge in my role is simply getting the word out internationally about what was once the best kept secret in America.

“We have been a small- and now medium-sized state in the interior of America, and not enough people abroad have heard the ‘why Utah’ story.”

Cox hinted at more official engagements with Singapore in the months ahead.

“We would encourage our friends in Singapore to come and visit us, and we need to go visit our friends in Singapore, so that they know that there are other options out there,” he said.

title: India's non-fossil fuel capacity crosses 300 GW, government says
description:
The growth in clean energy capacity has been driven by strong contributions from multiple sectors.
During 2025-26, India added a record 55.29 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity generation capacity, including 44.6 GW of solar power and 6 GW of wind power.
The rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity has also translated into higher generation.

text:
The Indian government has said the country has crossed 300 GW of non-fossil fuel-based installed electricity generation capacity, reaching more than 60% of the 500 GW target set for 2030.

The share of non-fossil fuel-based capacity in India’s total installed electricity generation capacity, which currently stands at around 552 GW, has risen to more than 54%, according to a government statement.

“Backed by the key policy enablers provided by the government for this transformation, this monumental achievement highlights India’s rapid progress towards building an Aatmanirbhar energy ecosystem and securing the target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030,” the statement said.

The growth in clean energy capacity has been driven by strong contributions from multiple sectors. Solar power remains the key growth engine, with installed capacity reaching around 165 GW, up from just 2.8 GW in 2014.

The wind energy sector has also recorded significant growth, with installed capacity crossing 58 GW, compared with 21 GW in 2014.

During 2025-26, India added a record 55.29 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity generation capacity, including 44.6 GW of solar power and 6 GW of wind power.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity has also translated into higher generation. Renewable energy generation increased from 190.96 billion units (BU) in 2014-15 to 477.79 BU in 2025-26, according to the government.

To support this expansion and strengthen domestic supply chains, India has also significantly expanded its renewable energy manufacturing capabilities. Driven by the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, which focuses on high-efficiency, domestically manufactured solar modules, the enlisted capacity under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) for solar PV modules has crossed the 200 GW milestone, up from just 2.3 GW in 2014.

The government said the clean energy transition is no longer limited to climate commitments but has become central to strengthening India’s industrial competitiveness, energy security and economic resilience.

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) is also advancing industrial decarbonisation through the National Green Hydrogen Mission, with the aim of positioning India as a global hub for the production, use and export of green hydrogen and its derivatives.

But those reviews, conducted through DOD’s Military Aviation and Installation Assurance Siting Clearinghouse, have not been occurring since April, claim developers, states and proponent groups, who described the stoppage as a politically motivated, de facto moratorium, according to federal district court Judge Karin Immergut's ruling. The Aug. 6 opinion ordered an injunction while a federal lawsuit proceeds.

The order mentioned that at least 106 onshore and offshore wind projects in 21 states representing at least $47 billion in investment remain in approval limbo. That is the claim of the May 31 lawsuit brought by developers and clean energy groups that was joined last month by 18 states and Washington, D.C.

Noting that DOD has not complied with regulatory deadlines for security reviews, Immergut, appointed by President Donald Trump in 2019, stressed that the agency “cannot pick and choose which parts of this legal regime to follow,” ordering it to resume reviews and submit status reports every 30 days.

“For months, wind projects capable of supplying millions of homes and businesses with low-cost power have been needlessly obstructed, as electricity costs and demand soar,” Phelps Turner, senior attorney for U.S. clean energy at the Environmental Defense Fund, said in a statement.

Plaintiffs argue that before stopping the reviews, DOD did not alert any projects to special risks and that its broad halt of all projects is unlawful, creating delays that could cause them to miss federal tax credit deadlines and risk investor pullout or cancellation.

In oral arguments and other statements, DOD claimed the review pause was part of a new assessment of risks “actively evaluating land-based wind energy projects to ensure they do not impair national security or military operations.” In a media statement last month, DOD said it was “actively evaluating” projects in a complex process “to balance renewable energy development with the protection and preservation of testing, training, and operational readiness.”

Developer RWE Latest to Ink Fed Lease Deal

Federal judges have rejected other administration moves to restrict the sector, overturning in rapid succession in January and February Trump stop-work directives against five offshore Atlantic coast projects that now are completely or largely built.

As such, the administration appears to be having more success using direct payouts to developers to have them revoke leases for prospective wind projects,

German energy developer RWE became the latest target, with the firm announcing Aug. 6 that it would give up leases won in Biden-era auctions for sites off New York, California and Louisiana in return for a $1.22-billion federal refund—the largest package so far. Those projects were in early stages of development. “After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future,” the company said. The agreement resolves RWE's claims against the U.S. government, but the firm did not address whether the payment covers its lease payments and other development costs.

The company will invest about the same amount in new U.S. natural gas projects, but told industry publication Recharge that it was not specifically required to. “RWE determines where and how to deploy capital across its energy portfolio based on where it can deliver the greatest, more immediate value,” a company spokesperson told the publication.

RWE said it remains a leader in renewable energy outside the U.S. with 18 offshore wind farms operating, four under construction and others in development—including 6.9 GW of capacity secured in the most recent U.K. wind auction.

The developer's agreement to exit its U.S. leases makes it one of six to do so, with a total of nearly $4 billion in refunds. “These buyouts are not one-for-one ‘swaps’ for another kind of energy,” said Hillary Bright, executive director of wind advocacy group Turn Forward. “When you eliminate future utility-scale power sources from busy population centers, you need a clear Plan B to avoid future grid stress. Replacing coastal offshore wind with LNG in Louisiana does nothing to address rising ratepayer affordability concerns, reliability challenges, or potential gaps in power supply in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic.”

Seven Democratic-run states, including New York, sued the administration in June over the first deal with France-based TotalEnergies. California has also sent a notice of intent to sue over two cancelled projects off the state’s central coast.

Dominion Wind Project's Mixed Results

Meanwhile, while Virginia utility Dominion Energy and its would-be buyer, NextEra Energy, are optimistic that the former’s 2.6-GW Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, the largest in the U.S., will provide returns when finished, CEO Robert Blue acknowledged Aug. 7 that administration tariffs on imported components are a factor in the project's increased cost hikes.

Project cost has risen to about $11.7 billion, up $288 million from its most recent cost estimate in April, he revealed in Dominion's latest results, citing “costs associated with revisions to prior steel and aluminum guidance.” Tariffs raised costs for imported steel, aluminum and copper by 50%, he said. Other cost factors included revised network upgrade costs assigned by grid operator PJM Interconnection. The company also said it estimates it will complete all work on the project by the end of 2027, extended from early next year.

The project uses mostly imported components, including 176 Siemens Gamesa 14.7-MW turbines and monopiles made in Germany.

Blue said 31 turbines with a capacity of more than 450 MW are installed “averaging approximately two days of operations per installation from jack up to jack down, in line with our prior assumptions [and] rivaling the magnitude of some of our fossil units.”

Dominion has already used the wind power to help meet record demand peaks set this summer in Virginia, he noted. “This allows the project to clearly demonstrate technical feasibility and deliver energy to the grid well before the final turbine begins to spin,” Blue stated.

Dominion also will begin seeking state and federal approvals in its next quarter for the NextEra Energy merger that could reach financial close by the end of 2027.

text:
New Zealand Steel has begun commercial steel production using a new electric arc furnace (EAF) at its Glenbrook steelworks, marking a major shift in the company’s manufacturing operations and reducing the site’s annual greenhouse gas emissions by more than 45%, according to the company.

In a news release, the steelmaker said the first commercial heat was produced just over two years after construction began in June 2024.

The transition involved replacing Glenbrook’s oxygen steelmaking furnace and two of its four coal-fuelled kilns, which New Zealand Steel said will halve coal use at the site.

Robin Davies, chief executive Australia and New Zealand at New Zealand Steel, described the first production as a significant milestone for the business.

“The project has exceeded a million hours of construction effort to get us to this point today,” Davies said.

Davies said the new EAF would create opportunities to expand the use of lower-carbon steel in New Zealand, including in construction and infrastructure.

“We’ve produced the first heat just over 2 years after breaking ground and been able to undertake this significant business transition within a fully operational steelworks, continuing to produce the usual 650,000 tonnes of steel to ensure uninterrupted supply to the domestic sectors that rely on it,” he said.

The EAF uses locally supplied scrap steel and electricity from renewable generation. New Zealand Steel said agreements with scrap suppliers Sims and GMS would redirect hundreds of thousands of tonnes of scrap from export markets to domestic recycling at Glenbrook.

Contact Energy is also supplying firmed renewable electricity under an agreement supporting the furnace’s operations, according to New Zealand Steel.

The project includes up to $140 million in co-investment from the New Zealand Government. Davies said the investment demonstrated the importance of partnerships in delivering projects of this scale.

“Projects of this scale rely on partnerships and this one is a world-class example of a successful public private investment partnership with the New Zealand government co-investing up to $140m,” he said.

New Zealand Steel said the transition was completed while the Glenbrook steelworks remained operational, allowing the company to continue supplying its domestic customers.

The company’s sister business, Pacific Steel, is expected to be the first to bring steel produced through the new process to market. New Zealand Steel said its PACIFIC™ product would be introduced later this year, while PACIFIC DCRB® reinforcing steel is intended to provide a lower-carbon option for locally manufactured reinforcement products.

New Zealand Steel said the project was intended to support the long-term future of domestic steel manufacturing while reducing the emissions associated with production.

title: The view from the proving grounds for next-generation nuclear reactors, Atomic City, Idaho
description:
People still smoke indoors at the bar in Atomic City, Idaho, population 52.
After stalling out for decades, nuclear power is having a moment.
President Donald Trump fast-tracked new projects, and now a new generation of small nuclear reactors is poised to come online in the next few years.
said Edwin Lyman, Nuclear Power Safety Director at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
A majority of Americans oppose new nuclear plants near them, but polling also shows growing support for the U.S. "emphasizing" nuclear power more broadly.
text:
People still smoke indoors at the bar in Atomic City, Idaho, population 52. The walls are plastered with one dollar bills and a Don't Tread On Me flag.

"Where were you Monday?" bar and nearby race track owner Vickie O'Haro asks one of her regulars.

O'Haro knows her customers orders without asking: cold beers or shots called atomic bombs — fitting since most of her customers work down the road at Idaho National Laboratory, or INL, America's nuclear energy testgrounds since 1949.

A March Gallup poll shows a majority of Americans still oppose a nuclear energy plant in their area, but that's not the case here

" I live 10 miles away, and I'm fine," O'Haro said. "I'm not glowing in the dark, you know? There's nothing to be scared of."

After stalling out for decades, nuclear power is having a moment. President Donald Trump fast-tracked new projects, and now a new generation of small nuclear reactors is poised to come online in the next few years.

Three companies at INL — and one in central Utah — switched on new types of reactors this summer.

" I think it's actually pretty cool to be happening in my backyard," O'Haro said.

Zoom out and INL is a pretty big backyard. It's 900 square miles of remote, sagebrush-filled high desert, almost the size of Rhode Island.

Electricity demand is skyrocketing

And it's in an unassuming building here that one startup, Deployable Energy, recently took its test reactor "critical." That means it had a sustained chain reaction for the first time, proving the design works and could someday generate electricity.

Lance Maul, chief operating officer at Deployable Energy, described this as a "real moment in history for the nation."

"This could be a real turning point for the energy future," said Maul, who has an Australian accent and was sporting a scraggly beard and a man bun.

He said the goal isn't your 20th century reactor: massive, expensive nuclear plants. It's micro reactors, which could power a thousand homes versus a million.

"It's something deployable," Maul said. "it's something that you can put on the back of a truck. It is a fundamentally different proposition."

Nuclear optimists like Maul see a future where these reactors are mass produced and power remote communities, military bases and AI data centers. They see them as a solution to meet America's rising energy demand without emitting carbon.

Trump is also a fan. Last year, the Department of Energy sped up reactor permitting. NPR reporting has shown that means getting rid of hundreds of pages of regulations, without telling the public.

Looser federal regulations

"I have no confidence in the Department of Energy and its oversight of this at all." said Edwin Lyman, Nuclear Power Safety Director at the Union of Concerned Scientists.

He said he worries about reduced standards around radiation, security and environmental contamination.

Plus, according to ProPublica reporting, the federal commission that oversees commercial nuclear development has lost hundreds of staff, especially safety experts, due to cuts by the Trump administration and resignations. Companies now testing their reactors will seek approval from that commission.

"I don't think cutting corners when you're talking about nuclear safety is a good idea," Lyman said. "I'm concerned about its impact on the communities around INL"

But at the bar in Atomic City, where lab workers drink after a long day, O'Haro said she's not worried.

" If we weren't safe, my guys would tell me that we weren't safe." she said, before turning up the country music playing in the background.

A majority of Americans oppose new nuclear plants near them, but polling also shows growing support for the U.S. "emphasizing" nuclear power more broadly.

text:
Los Angeles is moving ahead with a controversial energy project that critics say could lock residents into decades of higher costs and continued pollution.

On Aug. 4, the Los Angeles City Council voted to allow the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power to continue with a roughly $1 billion plan to retrofit the Scattergood plant so it can burn a mix of hydrogen and natural gas.

What happened?

According to CleanTechnica, the appeal challenging LADWP's environmental review failed on a 10-3 vote.

Councilmembers Katy Yaroslavsky, Nithya Raman, and Eunisses Hernandez backed the appeal, while Councilmember Hugo Soto-Martinez did not take part because he has investments connected to hydrogen energy, the outlet reported.

At the center of the dispute is whether Scattergood is truly a climate-friendly bridge project or simply another gas plant with a cleaner label. LADWP announced the retrofit plan in 2022, saying the facility would be capable of using a hydrogen-and-methane blend as the city works toward its 100% renewable energy mandate by 2035.

Critics also question the project's hydrogen promise because the Angeles Link hydrogen pipeline project has collapsed.

Without that supply, they argue, communities such as Inglewood, Hawthorne, and Lennox could remain burdened by fossil fuel infrastructure without getting the clean-energy benefits they were promised.

Explaining her vote, Yaroslavsky said that while "as recently as May of this year, the department publicly committed to reaching 2,220 MW of local solar by 2035, … DWP isn't close to meeting that goal."

Why does it matter?

To opponents, the price tag matters as much as the fuel choice. They argue that putting $1 billion into gas infrastructure could increase costs for residents while slowing investment in cleaner options such as local solar and battery storage.

Ben Harris of Los Angeles Waterkeeper, a senior staff attorney focused on regulatory affairs and legal policy, warned that hydrogen production is "incredibly water intensive" at a time when many Angelenos are already worried about water reliability. He also said the city has other ways to protect the grid while continuing to pursue its clean-energy targets.

There is also a financial risk. As the economy shifts away from fossil fuels, major investments tied to gas can become liabilities instead of engines of growth. Fossil fuel businesses and projects are increasingly vulnerable to underperformance as clean energy technologies expand, create jobs, and offer more durable economic upside.

For a public utility, that can translate into stranded assets, burdens for ratepayers, and less resilience.

Health impacts are another major concern. Opponents argue the project would extend pollution in communities that have already spent years coping with poor air quality linked to fossil fuel infrastructure.

What's being done?

A coalition of groups — Sierra Club, Los Angeles Waterkeeper, Food & Water Watch, Communities for a Better Environment, Physicians for Social Responsibility — Los Angeles, and the Center for Biological Diversity — pushed the appeal and continues to argue for a different path.

Their alternative is to speed up investment in proven technologies instead of betting on a hydrogen supply that may not arrive.

Harris said Los Angeles could preserve grid reliability through "investments in local solar and storage," which supporters say would better align with the city's 2035 renewable-energy goal.

Advocates say that approach could also bring benefits, including more local clean-energy jobs, lower exposure to volatile fossil fuel costs, and a stronger case for economic resilience.

"The City Council just hit residents with 50 years of higher rates to pay for a fossil-fueled facility that will be obsolete the day it opens," said David Pettit, a senior attorney with the Climate Law Institute at the Center for Biological Diversity.

Andrea Vega, the Los Angeles organizing manager for Food & Water Watch, said, "Angelenos want and deserve safe, clean air, and affordable energy."

title: EV Industry To Create 40 Million Jobs By 2030, Pay 45% More: Report - NDTV
description:
New Delhi: India's electric vehicle story is no longer just about what people will drive.
India's EV industry could create 30 million to 40 million jobs by 2030, according to Adecco India.
The study adds that most EV jobs may not be in car factories.
Adecco India estimates that only around 10-15 per cent of the 30-40 million jobs will be direct jobs.
Adecco India estimates that specialised EV talent could command salary premiums of up to 45 per cent compared with traditional internal-combustion-engine roles.
text:
New Delhi:

India's electric vehicle story is no longer just about what people will drive. It is increasingly about who will build, charge, service, manage and recycle those vehicles.

India's EV industry could create 30 million to 40 million jobs by 2030, according to Adecco India. And a surprisingly large share of these jobs may not be in traditional automobile factories.

Battery manufacturing, charging infrastructure, fleet operations, software, vehicle servicing and battery recycling are expected to become some of the biggest sources of new employment. Adecco India expects hiring in the sector to grow 15-20 per cent annually, with demand for specialised roles rising by around 35 per cent.

The study adds that most EV jobs may not be in car factories. Adecco India estimates that only around 10-15 per cent of the 30-40 million jobs will be direct jobs. The remaining 85-90 per cent will be indirect jobs.

This means the employment opportunity will extend far beyond people assembling electric cars, scooters and three-wheelers. Think charging stations. Battery maintenance. Fleet management. Software. Telematics. Customer support. Vehicle servicing. Driver training. Logistics. Battery recycling.

Manufacturing is still expected to remain the biggest employment engine, accounting for around 50-55 per cent of total EV hiring demand, according to Adecco India. But three areas are likely to grow particularly fast: battery manufacturing, EV infrastructure and the circular economy.

India's current EV adoption numbers already show why this ecosystem is expanding. The government's PM E-DRIVE dashboard showed more than 12.6 lakh electric two-wheelers and three-wheelers registered or temporarily registered under the scheme in 2025-26, as of July 2026. The current financial year has also seen more than 6.4 lakh such vehicles in the dashboard data as of July 27.

EV Job Market Landscape

The next EV job boom may not necessarily be restricted to the traditional automobile centres. Delhi's Rs 7,000-crore EV push shows where this is heading The Delhi EV Policy 2026 came into force on July 1. It includes purchase and scrappage incentives, charging infrastructure and tax and registration benefits for eligible EVs.

The policy is also more aggressive than simply offering subsidies. It also envisages around 30,000 charging points across the city. That has implications for jobs. Every new charger needs installation and maintenance. Every growing EV fleet needs technicians, operators and managers. Every electric vehicle eventually needs servicing. The EV economy, therefore, grows around the vehicle.

There is another reason this transition could be attractive to workers. Adecco India estimates that specialised EV talent could command salary premiums of up to 45 per cent compared with traditional internal-combustion-engine roles.

Companies may have access to people who understand conventional automobile engineering. But they increasingly need workers who understand batteries, power electronics, software, charging systems and connected mobility. And those skills are still relatively scarce.

Deepesh Gupta, Director and Head of General Staffing at Adecco India, said India's long-term opportunity lies in capturing a larger share of the global EV value chain. He pointed to India's growing presence in electric mobility, noting that the country currently contributes around 4 per cent of the global passenger-car EV industry and has a 17 per cent market share in two-wheelers.

But Gupta said India's competitiveness will depend as much on its talent pipeline as on manufacturing capacity. He also called for faster reskilling of conventional automobile workers, stronger industry-academia partnerships and greater investment in specialised technical education.

Naveen Gupta, Founder and CEO of Trev Mobility, sees the opportunity even more broadly. He said India's EV transition is not simply about replacing petrol and diesel vehicles with electric ones. It is about building an entirely new economic ecosystem around mobility.

From his company's experience, he said scaling an electric fleet requires people across operations, technology, driver training, charging management and service delivery. And that list will only grow.

As commercial fleets shift to EVs, companies will need people who can monitor battery performance, manage charging schedules, optimise routes and keep vehicles on the road. Software and telematics will become increasingly important too.

Contract Jobs Could Be First Step

Adecco India expects around 40-50 per cent of new hiring mandates to initially come through contractual and flexi-staffing arrangements before some of those roles become permanent. So the EV job boom may not immediately arrive in the form of millions of permanent payroll positions.

text:
While the global electric vehicle market outside China grew more than 30% in the first half of this year, Chinese EV makers are rapidly reshaping the competitive landscape with explosive overseas sales growth. Hyundai Motor Group, despite posting double-digit sales gains, was overtaken by BYD's aggressive push and fell to fourth place.

According to SNE Research, a Seoul-based energy market research firm, a total of 4.598 million battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) were delivered to markets worldwide excluding China during the January-to-June period of 2026. That represents a 30.3% increase from 3.529 million units in the same period a year earlier. By contrast, the overall global EV market — including China — grew just 5.5%, signaling that the center of gravity for electrification is rapidly shifting from China's domestic market to non-China regions.

By automaker, Volkswagen Group held onto the top spot with 635,000 units sold. While that marked a 7.6% increase year-over-year, the German giant underperformed the broader market, causing its market share to drop 2.9 percentage points from 16.7% to 13.8%. Tesla ranked second with 599,000 units, a 31.0% jump from a year earlier, buoyed by a second-quarter sales recovery. The U.S. EV maker held its market share steady at 13.0%.

The most striking shift was the surge of Chinese automakers. BYD aggressively expanded its overseas sales network across Europe, Southeast Asia, and Latin America, delivering 497,000 units — an 81.4% leap — to vault into third place. Its market share climbed 3.0 percentage points from 7.8% to 10.8%, reaching a level that now threatens Volkswagen and Tesla.

Hyundai Motor Group delivered 370,000 units in the first half, growing 25.9% year-over-year, but fell short of the non-China market's average growth rate of 30.3%, slipping from third to fourth place. While a recovery in European EV sales and an expanded electrified lineup drove volume gains, Chinese rivals grew at a far faster clip. Hyundai Motor Group's market share also edged down from 8.3% to 8.0%.

China's Geely Group ranked fifth with 296,000 units, up 47.0%, while Chery Automobile rode its export-focused brands Omoda and Jaecoo to deliver 201,000 units — a staggering 350.7% surge — cracking the top 10 at ninth place. In contrast, BMW managed just a 3.8% increase to 268,000 units, and Stellantis saw deliveries decline 5.7% to 246,000 units, underscoring its struggles.

The table below summarizes first-half non-China EV delivery performance by major automaker.

AutomakerH1 2026 DeliveriesYoY ChangeMarket ShareVolkswagen Group635,000+7.6%13.8%Tesla599,000+31.0%13.0%BYD497,000+81.4%10.8%Hyundai Motor Group370,000+25.9%8.0%Geely Group296,000+47.0%6.4%BMW268,000+3.8%5.8%Stellantis246,000-5.7%5.4%Chery Automobile201,000+350.7%4.4%

Note: Delivery figures are rounded; market share is calculated against the total non-China market of 4.598 million units.

By region, Europe solidified its position as the largest market, recording 2.528 million units — a 29.0% increase year-over-year — driven by stricter emissions regulations and new model launches. The region accounted for 55.0% of the total non-China EV market. Asia excluding China posted the fastest growth, surging 75.8% to 933,000 units, fueled by simultaneous new vehicle launches and expanded local production in India and Thailand. The region's market share jumped from 15.0% to 20.3%.

North America, however, was the weakest region, with deliveries falling 20.5% year-over-year to just 681,000 units. The decline reflected the expiration of U.S. EV tax credits, elevated vehicle prices, and model changeovers at some manufacturers. North America's market share plummeted 9.5 percentage points from 24.3% to 14.8%.

"The trajectory of non-China market share in the second half will hinge on the sustainability of European market growth, how long the incentive vacuum persists in North America, and the pace at which Chinese automakers localize production in Asia," an SNE Research representative said.

Industry observers note that as Chinese automakers rapidly capture non-China market share with value-focused models, Hyundai Motor Group needs to accelerate its affordable EV lineup alongside building out its North American local production infrastructure. Should the aggressive overseas expansion led by BYD and Chery continue into the second half, competition in the global EV market is expected to intensify further.

title: Who should build the low-carbon economy? - Academia - The Jakarta Post
description:
And where competences complement one another, governments could engage in mutually beneficial collaborations, mobilizing scientists, technology and manufacturing toward common goals.
But only two of these economies, Japan and South Korea, managed to join the exclusive club of so-called original equipment manufacturers.
Nonetheless, with the rise and spread of the clean-energy industry and other climate technologies, many thought that history could be written differently.
But the geographical diversification of technological innovation has remained more of a dream than a reality.

text:
But one can also imagine a more optimistic scenario. Since each country would understand its own challenges best, it could devise solutions adapted to its own circumstances, building systems and equipment at precisely the scale required. And where competences complement one another, governments could engage in mutually beneficial collaborations, mobilizing scientists, technology and manufacturing toward common goals.

Unfortunately, humankind has tended in the opposite direction. Since the first Industrial Revolution and the emergence of a truly global economy around the turn of the 19th century, goods and technologies have reached the farthest corners of the world, but the ability to design, build, market and extract value from them has remained highly concentrated.

By the mid-1800s, steam locomotives were already operational in almost 60 countries or colonies, yet only Britain, the United States, and certain German states were fully capable of supplying them. Telegraphic lines followed a similarly uneven pattern, as did the auto industry, which emerged at the turn of the 20th century and became emblematic of globalization in the post-World War II era with the internationalization of manufacturing capabilities, especially in large developing countries in Asia and Latin America. But only two of these economies, Japan and South Korea, managed to join the exclusive club of so-called original equipment manufacturers.

With the end of the Cold War, the information-technology industry took this model, under the banner of “Designed in California, assembled in China”, to the next level, drawing a clear line between knowledge-intensive, well-remunerated activities and labor-intensive, low-paid operational ones.

Nonetheless, with the rise and spread of the clean-energy industry and other climate technologies, many thought that history could be written differently. When China started to gain global market share in the production of solar panels and wind turbines, some analysts suggested that “green windows of opportunity” could emerge across the rest of the developing world. Having successfully learned the inner workings of the new technologies through joint ventures and licensing agreements with advanced-economy providers, China seemed to have found a blueprint that others could follow.

But the geographical diversification of technological innovation has remained more of a dream than a reality. The International Energy Agency finds that while clean-energy technologies are spreading fast, with solar capacity having increased tenfold since 2015, manufacturing capabilities remain highly concentrated.

text:
A group of 16 graduate students has delivered on a challenge BMW set them two years ago: build an electric vehicle that generates more energy than it uses in everyday driving.

The result is the Deep Orange 17, a 550kg solar-skinned coupe unveiled last week at Clemson University in South Carolina and nicknamed the Luminetta. Modelled over a typical 20km daily urban commute, the prototype generated enough surplus solar energy to add an average of 50km of driving range, around two and a half times the commute itself.

The project came through Clemson’s Deep Orange programme, which has master’s students in automotive engineering design, engineer and build a working prototype alongside an industry partner. BMW, a founding partner of the university’s automotive research centre and sponsor of five Deep Orange projects, set the energy-positive brief in late 2024.

“This is a project we’ve wanted to pursue for years, so it’s incredibly rewarding to see this group of students come together over the last two years, overcome so many technical challenges and constraints, and bring an energy-positive vehicle to life,” says Stephan Augustin, BMW’s project manager of research and new technologies.

The car’s defining feature is its skin. More than 1,700 photovoltaic cells are integrated directly into the exterior surfaces, developed with Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems. Their construction keeps generating power even when sections are shaded, and a durable outer film, coloured using a laser manufacturing process, protects the lot. The body harvests energy whether the car is parked or moving, a nod to the reality that most passenger vehicles spend the bulk of their lives stationary.

Keeping the maths energy-positive demanded extreme efficiency everywhere else. At 550kg, the Luminetta weighs roughly a quarter of a comparable production car, built on a multi-material chassis mixing structural steel for occupant protection with aluminium, carbon fibre members and 3D-printed metal joints. The two-door body borrows its form from the boxfish, whose naturally low-drag shape preserves interior space, while regenerative braking, intelligent torque distribution and optimised drivetrain controls squeeze out the rest. No power or torque figures have been published; efficiency was the brief, not pace.

To validate the concept, the team modelled sunlight and climate conditions across four cities: Greenville in South Carolina, Frankfurt, Madrid and Mumbai. The 50km average surplus held across all four.

“This was an incredibly challenging project, not only to create a working energy-positive prototype, but to demonstrate how a vehicle can become increasingly energy independent through solar integration,” says Harsh Manghnani, the team’s solar integration lead.

Inside, a custom interface serves real-time telemetry alongside wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The 16 students graduated the day after the unveiling with Master of Science degrees in automotive engineering. Their car stays on at the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research as a rolling research platform, and is scheduled to appear at CES in Las Vegas in January.

Solar-assisted EVs have a chequered history of promising much and reaching production rarely, but as a proof of what integrated photovoltaics can do for a light, efficient commuter, the Luminetta makes the case about as clearly as it has yet been made.

name: Clean Energy
title: BMW Reduces X5 Emissions by 40% Through Sustainable Manufacturing Practices
description:
BMW is demonstrating that building a more environmentally friendly car involves far more than simply replacing a gasoline engine with an electric motor.
Taking the latest X5 as an example, the German automaker has redesigned numerous aspects of the vehicle manufacturing process, incorporating recycled materials, renewable energy, and circular production models, which it claims can reduce emissions by up to 40%.
At the material level, BMW has increased its use of aluminum semis produced with renewable energy, applying them to components such as wheel rims and brake calipers.
Meanwhile, aluminum scrap generated during production is systematically collected and reintroduced into the manufacturing process through a closed-loop recycling system.
BMW states that this series of changes has helped reduce carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions during the X5's product development process by about 40%, though this figure remains subject to independent third-party verification.
text:
BMW is demonstrating that building a more environmentally friendly car involves far more than simply replacing a gasoline engine with an electric motor. Taking the latest X5 as an example, the German automaker has redesigned numerous aspects of the vehicle manufacturing process, incorporating recycled materials, renewable energy, and circular production models, which it claims can reduce emissions by up to 40%.

At the material level, BMW has increased its use of aluminum semis produced with renewable energy, applying them to components such as wheel rims and brake calipers. Meanwhile, aluminum scrap generated during production is systematically collected and reintroduced into the manufacturing process through a closed-loop recycling system. According to the company, roughly one-third of the total weight of the iX5 60 xDrive, approximately 940 kg, comes from secondary raw materials, effectively reducing dependence on newly extracted resources.

BMW states that this series of changes has helped reduce carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions during the X5's product development process by about 40%, though this figure remains subject to independent third-party verification.

China's strong push toward an energy transition and green, low-carbon development is not just reshaping its domestic economy — it is creating massively scaled, entirely new collaborative opportunities for the global market.

Industry leaders say China is acting as a powerful locomotive, using this mandate to open a "green cooperation door" for global businesses.

"The policy blueprint laid out for the 15th Five-Year Plan has further bolstered our confidence in China's long-term market prospects," said Karen Yin, president of AkzoNobel China.

Yin noted that the market's steady high-level opening-up allows foreign enterprises to fully tap into these new ecological priorities. This green transition perfectly embodies the core of this new era — China's development is generating a "blue ocean" of incremental growth, forging a pathway for mutual, cross-border industrial prosperity.

From urban transit and commercial real estate to heavy chemical manufacturing and maritime shipping, the application scenarios for China's green transition are expanding at a breakneck pace. For multinational companies, this translates not only to clearer policy expectations but also to vastly broader commercial horizons.

The physical manifestations of this shift are already visible across the country.

description:
The global electric vehicle market, excluding China, showed steep growth in the first half of this year.
As demand for electric vehicles surged rapidly, especially in Europe and Asia, the overall market growth far outpaced previous rates.
This far exceeded the total global electric vehicle market growth rate of 5.5% during the same period.
EV sales grew rapidly in major markets such as India and Thailand, with 933,000 units delivered in the first half.
Geely also posted substantial gains with 296,000 units delivered, up 47.0%, and Chery delivered 201,000 units, a staggering 350.7% increase.
text:
The global electric vehicle market, excluding China, showed steep growth in the first half of this year. As demand for electric vehicles surged rapidly, especially in Europe and Asia, the overall market growth far outpaced previous rates. In contrast, the North American market saw a double-digit decline due to the end of U.S. electric vehicle tax incentives. Notably, the overseas sales of Chinese automakers such as BYD and Chery soared, quickly reshaping the competitive landscape outside China.

According to SNE Research's “Global Monthly EV & Battery Tracker for July 2026” released on August 10, global electric vehicle (BEV and PHEV) deliveries excluding China from January to June this year reached 4,598,000 units, up 30.3% from 3,529,000 units in the same period last year. This far exceeded the total global electric vehicle market growth rate of 5.5% during the same period.

By region, Europe recorded the highest sales, delivering 2,528,000 units. This represented a 29.0% increase from the same period last year, accounting for 55.0% of all sales in markets outside China. The recovery in demand for electric vehicles in Europe was driven by the tightening of European Union emission regulations, new model launches, and various national incentive policies.

The strongest growth was seen in non-Chinese Asia. EV sales grew rapidly in major markets such as India and Thailand, with 933,000 units delivered in the first half. This marks a 75.8% increase compared to a year ago. The market share also rose by 5.3 percentage points, from 15.0% to 20.3%. The price competitiveness of Chinese companies and the expansion of local production in Southeast Asia are considered key contributors to this growth.

In contrast, North America showed the opposite trend. Deliveries in the first half totaled 681,000 units, a decline of 20.5%, while the regional share within non-Chinese markets plunged by 9.5 percentage points, from 24.3% to 14.8%. Analysts attribute this to increased purchasing burdens after the expiration of U.S. tax credits for new and used eco-friendly vehicles and commercial vehicles in September last year, as well as high vehicle prices and model transitions by some automakers.

In terms of company competition, Volkswagen maintained its top position with 635,000 units delivered. While this represented a 7.6% increase from last year, it fell far short of the market's average growth rate, resulting in a market share decline of 2.9 percentage points, from 16.7% to 13.8%.

Tesla ranked second with 599,000 units delivered, up 31.0% from last year. Its market share held steady at 13.0%, similar to last year. Q2 deliveries recovered to 480,126 vehicles, helping to boost its first-half performance. However, intensified competition with both Chinese and local brands in Europe, and weaker policy support in North America, mean Tesla’s growth in the second half will depend on its pricing and new model strategies.

Growth by Chinese automakers was even more pronounced. BYD maintained third place with 497,000 units, surging 81.4% year-over-year. Its market share expanded by 3.0 percentage points, from 7.8% to 10.8%, reflecting its rapidly expanded sales base in Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central/South America.

Geely also posted substantial gains with 296,000 units delivered, up 47.0%, and Chery delivered 201,000 units, a staggering 350.7% increase. Chery’s overseas expansion, led by export brands such as Omoda and Jaecoo, was identified as a key growth driver. Toyota climbed into the top ranks with 184,000 units, marking a 44.0% increase.

Hyundai Motor Group delivered 370,000 units, a 25.9% increase year-over-year. Revival in European EV demand and an expanded electrified lineup drove the increase, but since growth lagged behind the market average, its share slipped slightly from 8.3% to 8.0%. BMW delivered 268,000 units, only a 3.8% increase, while Stellantis saw deliveries drop by 5.7% to 246,000 units.

Divergences in regional growth rates are expected to play a key role in shaping the market in the second half. Non-Chinese Asia’s 75.8% growth has propelled it into a new core market, while North America registered a decline due to a lack of policy support. In particular, Chinese automakers are rapidly expanding into Asia and Europe with competitive pricing and local manufacturing, intensifying competition with established global automakers.

Industry analysts forecast that the prospects for the non-Chinese electric vehicle market in the second half will be determined by whether Europe can sustain its growth, the continuation or absence of incentives in North America, and the pace at which Chinese companies localize in overseas markets. The market is now entering a phase in which not only overall growth but also the question of which region, in what price range, and by which supplier will determine market leadership.
