text:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Africa’s largest economies are accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity, a shift industry analysts say reflects both industrial ambition and growing unease over dependence on imports from China that dominate the global market.

Ethiopia, South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria have been stepping up efforts to localize manufacturing of equipment for solar power, from module assembly to more advanced manufacturing, according to industry experts.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

However, they say China is likely to retain its dominant global role in making solar cells and other components. Its exports of such equipment have soared, partly due to a glut in supply back home.

Chinese renewable energy investment and related construction projects in Africa reached $66 billion between 2010 and 2024, according to the think tank ODI Global.

“Growing economies, coupled with recent energy shortages in countries like Zambia and the ongoing need to provide access to underserved populations, make it (Africa) a perfect market for China to channel its overcapacity in the sector,” said Olena Borodyna, a senior geopolitical risk advisor with the London-based think tank.

Africa eyes solar production

Africa's largest economies are keen to build their own solar manufacturing capacity.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

South Africa's utility, Eskom, plans to develop a 1-gigawatt solar manufacturing facility to capture more value from its fast-expanding solar market and respond to changing electricity demand.

Production of solar panels in Nigeria, meanwhile, is expanding rapidly, with local assembly capacity rising from about 120 megawatts to roughly 300 megawatts in the last two years. Its annual solar imports, mostly from China, also put it near South Africa’s level.

The homegrown manufacturing push is tied to structural shifts in Africa’s power markets. Rising adoption of rooftop and distributed solar systems in South Africa is reducing national grid demand, squeezing utilities’ revenues and prompting interest in diversification.

South Africa is already the continent’s largest importer of solar equipment, bringing in more than 3 gigawatts annually, also largely from China. Industry analysts say this scale of demand makes it one of the continent’s strongest candidates for localized production.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

African power markets shift

The increased interest in solar power represents a significant shift, said Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, even if actual manufacturing capacity remains limited. He said nations pursuing solar manufacturing tend to already have industrial capacity and strong domestic demand.

“Morocco has doubled production to around 1 gigawatt a year. South Africa maintains a similar capacity. Egypt has gigawatt-scale projects coming online,” he said.

“A few years ago, local solar manufacturing was barely on the agenda anywhere in Africa,” Clarke said “It is now becoming a recognized pillar of industrial policy and green economic development.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The need for more solar or other renewable power has soared. The industry group GOGLA estimates that more than 10 million solar kits were sold across Africa in 2025, serving roughly 148 million people. This was a 10% increase compared to 2024, with much of that growth concentrated in East and West Africa.

The solar build-out is within a highly concentrated global supply chain dominated by China. Africa has effectively no commercial-scale solar cell manufacturing, meaning emerging assembly plants still must rely on imported Chinese components.

“Most new factories assemble imported Chinese components rather than produce the high-value solar cells and other upstream materials, leaving Africa dependent on foreign technology for the most sophisticated parts of the supply chain,” Clarke said.

Technology transfer remains limited

China’s investment is helping Africa build manufacturing capacity and technical skills.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It's a vital opportunity for technology transfer and job creation, ODI Global’s Borodyna said, “given China’s expertise in building out these technologies at scale.”

“China will play a huge role in the build-out of manufacturing capacity across the continent, as well as continue solar exports to the continent," she said.

Experts say the continent has yet to receive the deeper sharing of knowhow needed to develop its own fully integrated solar industry.

Reliance on China for solar supply is likely to remain high in regions including Africa, said Hannah Pitt, with the think tank Rhodium Group’s energy and climate practice.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Trade restrictions in the U.S. and Europe have led Chinese companies to invest more in other regions such as Africa and Southeast Asia, according to Rhodium Group. Ethiopia is a favored destination, with more than half of the announced investments since 2018 coming from Chinese sources, alongside Japanese investments.

Investments in South Africa, Nigeria and Morocco were mostly led by domestic companies or joint ventures with local participation, the think tank said.

Saturated Chinese markets push solar manufacturing overseas

Extensive state support and years of steady investments in green technology manufacturing have resulted in an oversupply of solar power equipment and falling prices in China, a key factor in its huge global market share, said Lauri Myllyvirta with the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

With the market oversupplied, several major Chinese solar manufacturers, including Longi and Jinko, made losses in the first three months of 2026. For such companies, shifting overseas may be the only way to stay in business.

Chinese firms pledged as much as $250 billion in overseas green manufacturing projects between 2011 and the first half of last year, according to an estimate by Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab’s “China’s Green Leap Outward” report.

Chinese solar exports doubled in March reaching a new monthly record, as 50 countries set all-time records for Chinese solar imports in a single month, according to Ember, a think tank.

“In terms of producing and manufacturing things — like solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles — really China is by far the lead in this race,” said Li Shuo, director of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s China Climate Hub. “I personally expect the dominance of China to be further cemented and not weakened over the coming years.”

Chan reported from Hong Kong. Associated Press journalist Anton L. Delgado contributed from Bangkok.

description:
We support this demand for greater transparency and accountability, and commend Governor Abbott on these important steps.
We believe any company building infrastructure at this scale should welcome the kind of audit Governor Abbott is now requiring.
Water: Our facilities minimize water usage Water is a shared resource, and we treat it that way.

text:
Earlier this week, Governor Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to audit every data center project in the state's interconnection queue, requiring clear disclosure of tax incentives, energy use, water use, and ownership before any new project moves forward.

We support this demand for greater transparency and accountability, and commend Governor Abbott on these important steps.

This isn’t a new position for us. Our position is consistent with the way we have always done business. As data center development has accelerated across Texas, so have questions from the communities hosting it: what effect will these sites have on their neighbors, who is actually paying for this growth, and who is watching to make sure the promises hold? We believe any company building infrastructure at this scale should welcome the kind of audit Governor Abbott is now requiring. These are fair questions, and every developer – Crusoe included – should be able to answer them clearly.

Energy: We pay our own way for power

For Crusoe, energy-first means planning a site's power from day one – building thoughtfully, in ways that benefit both the grid and the communities we enter, and not just building quickly. We seek out sources of abundant, underutilized energy so our workloads don't add pressure to local grids, and we've become a leader in deploying new power generation capacity to support digital infrastructure. We cover our own onsite generation and any infrastructure upgrades our projects require, so the cost of our growth doesn’t land on a neighbor's electric bill.

That's also why, earlier this year, we joined the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge alongside Governor Abbott and more than 200 other developers, utilities, and states – standing with these leaders to keep investing in America's innovation economy, creating jobs, and responsibly building the power the nation needs, without asking ratepayers to foot the bill. In Abilene, our new campus will run entirely on on-site generation and battery storage, built and paid for by Crusoe.

Water: Our facilities minimize water usage

Water is a shared resource, and we treat it that way. Our closed-loop cooling systems recirculate water in a sealed loop, using virtually none of it during normal operations – a design choice that lets a 200-megawatt Crusoe data center use less water annually than ten average U.S. households. We don't think transparency about that number should be optional, and we don't wait for a regulator to ask for it.

Jobs: We prioritize hiring local residents

Our projects have created more than 13,000 positions to date across high-tech, construction, and skilled trades. We offer those roles to local workers in host communities first, backed by partnerships with regional vocational programs and local school districts. We believe a data center’s long-term economic impact should benefit every student, taxpayer, and business in a community.

Investments: Our projects boost the local economy

We've invested more than $20B to date at the local level, through job creation, local sourcing, and tax contributions that fund schools, emergency services, career training, water infrastructure, and roads. Abilene's economy has grown alongside our investment there – in the past year, the City has permitted more than 1,500 new homes to keep pace, on top of the tax revenue the campus contributes.

When we ask a community for a tax incentive to help build a project, we believe in being transparent about those agreements. What they actually create are enforceable commitments we're accountable for, not a one-way tax break. We think those commitments should be spelled out clearly to the community. Typically the tax receipts to communities remain very large even after tax abatements are agreed. In fact Crusoe data center projects are often among the largest tax sources if not the single largest tax payer in the communities where we operate. In Abilene alone, our flagship campus is expected to generate up to 32% of the City's and up to 25% of Taylor County's current budgeted property tax revenue once fully built out. Tax revenues from our project in Claude are expected to nearly double Armstrong County’s operating budget next year.

Ownership: Founded and headquartered in the United States

Crusoe was founded in the United States, in 2018, and remains headquartered here today. We are vertically integrated: we employ hundreds of American workers in Crusoe’s own manufacturing facilities located in Colorado, Oklahoma, and Louisiana to build much of the electrical equipment and switchgear that power our data centers. We're proud that Crusoe jobs are helping build the industrial capacity America needs to win the global race for AI leadership.

Accountability

None of this works as a one-time announcement. We often put our commitments into binding agreements with the communities where we build. We follow strict environmental and safety standards. We also hire local community liaisons so concerns don't have to travel far to reach someone who can quickly act on them.

We've held ourselves to this standard from the start because we don't think it should be possible to build infrastructure at this scale any other way. Governor Abbott is right to hold companies to a high standard, and we're glad to be judged against it.

Texas has been an important partner in Crusoe's growth. And we look forward to continuing that partnership – bringing economic development, jobs, and responsible growth to Texas communities, with commitments built to last for the long term.

description:
Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s directive pausing new data center interconnections to the ERCOT grid has placed nearly one-fifth of the entire U.S. data center development pipeline at risk of delays, according to analysis from BloombergNEF (BNEF).
BNEF tracks approximately 50 GW of Texas data center projects, of which more than 70% remain in early stages.
The pause specifically affects nearly 49.8 GW, representing almost 20% of the U.S. data center pipeline of about 253 GW.

text:
Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s directive pausing new data center interconnections to the ERCOT grid has placed nearly one-fifth of the entire U.S. data center development pipeline at risk of delays, according to analysis from BloombergNEF (BNEF). The move, announced August 3, 2026, requires a comprehensive audit of energy use, water consumption, financing, ownership, and community impacts before any additional projects can advance.

Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and ERCOT to verify and audit all data centers in the interconnection queue. Projects that fail to comply must be denied grid connection. The order pauses related transmission planning, including ERCOT’s “Batch Zero” large-load study process that was set to begin notifications around August 7. ERCOT confirmed it is postponing Batch Zero and will seek a good-cause exception at the PUCT’s August 20 open meeting.

The ERCOT queue holds roughly 474 GW of large-load interconnection requests—more than five times the grid’s record peak demand of approximately 91 GW— with about 90% attributed to data centers. BNEF tracks approximately 50 GW of Texas data center projects, of which more than 70% remain in early stages. The pause specifically affects nearly 49.8 GW, representing almost 20% of the U.S. data center pipeline of about 253 GW.

BNEF forecasts only about 1.2 GW of total ERCOT data center capacity additions between the second quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. Delays in energization over this window could put billions of dollars of data center leasing revenue at risk. The firm estimates AI computing capacity can generate around $1.76 billion per gigawatt per month. Under a base-case assumption that 60% of the delayed capacity is AI-related, cumulative revenue losses could reach just over $8 billion by the first quarter of 2027. In a full-delay scenario with a 100% AI-compute mix, the figure rises toward $15 billion. Longer pauses raise the chance that the review extends into the 2027 Texas legislative session, where lawmakers could alter interconnection rules.

BNEF still projects roughly 8.25 GW of additional data center capacity coming online in ERCOT through 2030, lifting the total above 17 GW. However, the firm notes that the 2030 outlook could be revised significantly if Batch Zero proceeds smoothly—or if the audit introduces material delays. Many requested projects appear speculative; the gap between the 474 GW queue and more realistic tracked pipelines underscores the need for the verification process.

Impacts on Projects and Investors

The pause injects uncertainty into timelines for the bulk of early-stage projects. Real estate investors and developers holding land under option or purchase agreements tied to data center schedules face potential force majeure or change-in-law claims. Power generation and transmission investors financing infrastructure linked to large loads must reassess viability, security interests, and capital deployment. Hundreds of millions of dollars in grid deposits—often $50,000 per megawatt for Batch Zero eligibility—now sit in limbo without a clear path to approval.

Some market reaction was immediate. Shares of certain Texas-exposed powered-land developers and independent power producers declined sharply in the days after the announcement. Hyperscalers and technology companies planning Texas campuses or expansions must now evaluate new disclosure requirements on tax incentives, on-site generation plans, water sources and cooling technology, community mitigation measures, and ownership structures. Projects relying solely on behind-the-meter (on-site) generation rather than ERCOT interconnection are generally outside the pause’s scope and may continue advancing.

Industry groups such as the Data Center Coalition have urged a swift process that distinguishes serious, responsible projects from speculative ones, citing potential for substantial investment and job creation. At the same time, community opposition over water use in arid areas, noise, traffic, and quality-of-life effects has grown across counties and cities, contributing to the political pressure behind the audit.

Broader Implications for Consumers and the Energy System

Abbott framed the directive around protecting Texans’ safety, quality of life, affordable energy, grid reliability, and water resources. It builds on a June 2026 order requiring data centers to cover their own infrastructure costs so residential customers are not burdened. The audit examines whether projects provide their own power or depend heavily on the grid, projected electricity and water consumption, cooling methods, tax abatements or public assistance, and community safeguards.

For consumers, the pause aims to reduce near-term upward pressure on electricity rates and the risk of reliability shortfalls amid explosive load growth. ERCOT has previously warned that data center and other large-load demand could drive significant increases in statewide peak requirements. By filtering the queue, regulators hope to prioritize viable projects while preserving system stability.

Indirect effects could ripple into related infrastructure. Delayed grid connections may slow associated transmission investments and influence the timing of gas-fired generation or pipeline laterals planned to serve data center campuses, particularly in the Permian and other gas-rich regions where behind-the-meter solutions have proliferated. Texas already hosts a large share of announced behind-the-meter gas capacity for data centers, supported by existing pipeline infrastructure. A prolonged pause could shift more development toward these self-supplied models or to other states.

The action follows New York’s July 2026 temporary halt on certain hyperscale data center approvals and reflects a broader recalibration in both Republican- and Democratic-led states seeking to balance economic opportunity with grid, water, and community constraints. No fixed end date for the Texas review has been announced. ERCOT and the PUCT are implementing the directive while the industry assesses how long the uncertainty will last and what permanent policy changes, if any, may emerge in 2027.

As Texas remains one of the largest and fastest-growing U.S. data center markets, the outcome of this audit will shape not only local project pipelines but a meaningful share of national AI and cloud infrastructure deployment timelines.

text:
German energy developer RWE has agreed to surrender its offshore wind leases in the United States after securing a $1.22 billion settlement with federal authorities.

The deal resolves legal claims made by RWE U.S. Offshore against the federal government, effectively halting development across three key marine lease tracts.

The agreement covers offshore lease sites located off the coasts of New York, California, and Louisiana. RWE stated that while over $1 billion had been spent acquiring and planning the sites, permitting hurdles left no viable path forward in the American market for the foreseeable future.

This settlement represents the fifth major agreement between federal agencies and renewable energy companies seeking to cancel offshore wind developments.

Total federal commitments to buy out offshore wind lease agreements have now surpassed $3.9 billion across multiple corporate deals.

Under terms connected to the buyout, RWE will shift focus toward other American energy infrastructure investments.

The company plans to deploy capital into liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects and gas turbine infrastructure to support broader grid capacity expansion goals.

The cancelled projects include a major tract in the New York Bight, the Canopy Offshore Wind site located off northern California, and a designated parcel in the waters off Louisiana.

text:
Eriberto throws his head back with a laugh and shakes it as he tills his plot of land in the Peruvian Amazon, near the Cordillera Azul National Park in central Peru.

“That does not work here,” he says with a chuckle, responding to a question about why he doesn’t call his diverse forest garden “agroforestry”.

In the past, government officials promoted planting coffee or cacao in agroforestry systems near his community. But Eriberto Guerra and other Indigenous farmers in the town of Lamas say it hasn’t been effective enough and some have rejected the sustainable farming label.

“They promoted growing just one or two other food crops with some trees,” Guerra tells Mongabay. “But you need to plant dozens of species along with traditional plants. When one crop fails or doesn’t perform well in the local market, you need to have others to make up for it. And those others need to be the right crops, planted the right way, near the right plants.”

His forest garden attracts endemic bird species and wildlife researchers, and has sustained his family for a decade, he says.

“This is what is working,” Eriberto says.

To mark the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples and better understand the subtleties in biodiversity conservation and climate solutions implemented by people living at the frontlines, Mongabay interviewed nine Indigenous representatives from around the world.

In order, we spoke with:

Jenifer Lasimbang, an executive director of Indigenous Peoples of Asia Solidarity (IPAS) from Malaysia

Juan Carlos Jintiach, an executive secretary of the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities (GATC) from Ecuador

Olo Villalaz, a representative for the Guna General Congress from Panama

João Victor Pankararu, a youth coordinator for a regional Indigenous organization (APOINME) from Brazil

Abdi Akbar, a director of political participation expansion at the Indigenous Peoples’ Alliance of the Archipelago (AMAN) from Indonesia

Sara Omi Casama, a president of a women leaders group under under the Mesoamerican Alliance of Peoples and Forests (AMPB) from Panama

Joseph Itongwa Mukumo, a coordinator of an Indigenous forest management NGO (REPALEF) from the Democratic Republic of Congo

Toya Manchineri, a general coordinator of the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon (COIAB) on the Brazil-Peru border

Valéria Paye, an executive director of the Podáali Fund from Brazil

They discussed the community-led environment and climate solutions they see are working — and not — at a local level. We also discussed the factors that make a solution more likely to succeed and the nuances of implementing certain efforts.

These interviews have been translated into English and edited for length and clarity.

Jenifer Lasimbang, executive director of Indigenous Peoples of Asia Solidarity (IPAS) Fund and former assembly member in Malaysia’s Sabah State Legislative Assembly (North Borneo, Malaysia)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Jenifer Lasimbang: In my community, we already have a natural resource management system practiced by Indigenous people called the Tagal system. It is a way of conserving resources and ensuring they are used sustainably. It is practiced along rivers, where we have red zones, orange zones and green zones.

The green zone is where you can harvest resources. The orange or yellow zone is where there are certain conditions under which you can harvest fish. The red zone is the breeding area, where you cannot take any resources because it is completely protected.

We are fortunate that, after more than 10 years of advocacy, this system has now been adapted and enacted into law in my area [Sabah].

Community forestry is another example and, of course, rotational or shifting cultivation is another practice that is often misunderstood. These practices are actually very sustainable, but have not been studied enough or promoted properly. Most of the time, in many countries, Indigenous peoples are prohibited from practicing shifting cultivation.

Customary approaches to natural resource management are also directly related to how we sustainably harvest and maintain resources, whether they are river resources, marine resources or resources within our territories, because we’ve established a long-term relationship with nature.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community or in others?

Jenifer Lasimbang: One of the biggest factors is recognition.

If our basic rights, identity and our way of life are not recognized, are overlooked, then we will not have security of tenure over our territories and practices, whether it is natural resource management, our wellness programs or anything else.

I think finance is also changing now. Many of us are part of Indigenous-led funding mechanisms that allow direct access and provide real support.

We are also thinking about — we do not call it monetizing — and still developing ideas around how Indigenous bioeconomies can flourish if we create systems that generate monetary benefits. It is still about monetary gains, but the way we see it is that those gains should directly benefit our communities.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Jenifer Lasimbang: All those conservation concepts that have been imposed on us that disregard what we have already been doing and that do not fit local realities.

In many parts of the world, Indigenous peoples are still being driven away from their territories, while top-down conservation concepts continue to be imposed on us and our lands. I think some of these concepts, such as carbon offsetting and monetizing nature, will not work if they are developed without properly including Indigenous peoples. I was in a panel discussion where they said that it is expensive to maintain and monitor all these schemes. But that is because they don’t consult Indigenous peoples, and they don’t acknowledge or recognize the role that Indigenous peoples have played in maintaining these areas in the first place.

Mongabay: You very briefly mentioned some carbon projects not consulting communities. Are there any particular examples that come to mind?

Jenifer Lasimbang: Mongabay was the one that uncovered the Nature Conservation Agreement [NCA] in Sabah, created out of nowhere by our state government, that locked communities into a carbon deal. The NCA process was not done properly. There was no consultation with Indigenous communities. They did not even identify where the area was located. They simply said, “Okay, we’re going to sell this 2 million hectares of rainforest for trading.”

But we also have examples of carbon deals that work. The one that did work [with Bursa Carbon Exchange] went all the way to the Malaysia’s stock exchange for proper trading. That was the one we were involved in. The community was part of it and it can be done properly. It can work — but not the ones created by our own carbon cowboys.

Juan Carlos Jintiach, executive secretary of the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities (GATC) (Napo Province, Ecuador)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Juan Carlos Jintiach: Many years ago, my own people’s territory (Pueblo Shuar) wanted to reduce deforestation, stop illegal logging and prevent illegal mining. These activities were coming from outside our territory.

We brought our own proposal to the table to secure the land: We proposed Nunka pénker iisar/Nunka iwiarkatniu, which means well-being or good living for the people in our territory [in the Shuar language]. It’s like a Life Plan [Plan de vida, Indigenous-led management and self-governance tools for peoples in Ecuador].

This involved understanding our own data: How much forest we have, what ecosystems exist in our territory and how we monitor them. Through this contribution to the country, we participated and collaborated in a voluntary project called the “Socio Bosque” project.

This was the first example from our territory showing how Indigenous peoples, using our own capacities and without requiring large amounts of funding, are contributing to climate solutions and protecting ecosystems. We also helped make visible concepts such as high forest and low deforestation.

If we look further south, we see similar exercises where Indigenous peoples monitor the state of rivers, how many biodiversity hotspots exist and the presence of plants, birds, animals and other elements of the ecosystem.

This type of data allows us to understand the problems happening today, how much damage is occurring in the context of climate change and how these changes are affecting our territories. We call this Tarímiat Pujutaí Nunka. Tarímiat means the territory where you live.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Juan Carlos Jintiach: It is important to recognize that when international agreements, governments and major policies are developed, they need to be translated and connected in the right way.

There are many acronyms, ideas and global projects that sound very positive. We need to make an effort to translate these global dynamics, these acronyms and ideas, and match them with Indigenous peoples’ own cosmovisions [cosmic worldviews] and perceptions. We need to develop a dialogue between different languages and ways of understanding.

Sometimes this is avoided. Sometimes people do not want to discuss these issues because there are many challenges related to political dynamics and the way situations are understood and contextualized.

We need to recognize these communities and provide legal titles and recognition under laws and constitutions. In addition, when governments develop policies or projects, they must invite us and consult with us.

Whenever I have an idea, I invite families and sit down with them. We drink tea, we share and we talk. We discuss, “Let’s do this. Let’s do that. This is the problem.” It always has to be done with us. That is the way it should be.

Finally, projects need to support the generations that are coming. It is very sad that governments and policies do not pay enough attention to future generations, to children, youth, women and elders, because it represents the destruction of families and of communities. It is very special how generations are raised and how knowledge is transmitted through language and culture.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Juan Carlos Jintiach: My job and my responsibility is as executive secretary globally for GATC, but when I return home, I work with Mother Earth.

I work with my plants, my cocoa and my teas on my land. For me, any product from the forest must have permissions and many conditions. I have to pay for certification from the government every year to show it is organic and sustainable, and this certification is very expensive.

But I already have my own certification in my culture through a chakra [an ancestral agricultural system]. It means how I manage my small portion of land, with medicine, food, economy, knowledge, wisdom, culture and spirituality. This should also be recognized and connected with policies at the national and international levels, but it’s not.

We are building Indigenous economies and global alliances, showcasing what we can do with products such as macambo [Theobroma bicolor] and other fruits that provide food sovereignty and food health. But our processes must be better recognized. There must be equity.

Mongabay: What are the most common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

Juan Carlos Jintiach: I am very worried about the future — very worried. Many people try to divide Indigenous people, buy our support and prevent us from standing together. It is very sad to see this happening between Indigenous people themselves, with many different offers being made, similar to political situations. If we do not have solidarity, if we do not maintain our unity, the future will be very difficult for us.

Politicians come and say, “I am going to do this, I am going to do that.” Of course, they make promises, but these promises are often disconnected from reality. This has to change.

Also, when we talk about finance, it is almost treated as a taboo. There is this perception that Indigenous peoples should not touch money, that Indigenous peoples are not prepared and that everything will fail. These negative perceptions and narratives need to be reversed. We need to change the paradigm and change the narrative.

We need to continue creating opportunities. Even if I fail implementing a project I received funding for, does that mean all Indigenous peoples have failed? No. It means that a specific initiative did not succeed. Failure should not be used to judge Indigenous peoples as a whole.

Governments and wealthy countries also fail. Institutions fail. So, as human beings, we need to respect governance systems.

Olo Villalaz, representative for the Guna General Congress and co-founded TV Indígena (Guna Yala, Panama)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Olo Villalaz: Across all our territories in Mesoamerica [which extends from modern northwestern Mexico to El Salvador], what’s really important is addressing deforestation and illegal mining that is entering our territories.

The territories we have in Mesoamerica are part of the Mesoamerican Biological Corridor, which connects with the Amazon. This biological corridor exists within our territories, and we are the ones taking care of it.

Today, there is enormous pressure from deforestation and livestock expansion, especially in Nicaragua, as well as deforestation pressures in Panama.

We are protecting these lands through community surveillance. They also know when they can conduct fire prevention and maintenance activities. They know which periods are dry, when droughts may occur and when there is a greater risk of fires.

Using traditional knowledge, women are also highly focused on protecting seeds, especially native seeds, and medicinal plants. They play an extremely important role in sustaining life within our territories and ensuring that future generations continue to be protected.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Olo Villalaz: Apart from land tenure, another factor we are looking into is new tools. For example, we are using drones and other new technologies. The idea is that we need to use these tools to our advantage.

Many territories are using these new technologies for monitoring. In the past, we had to walk for many kilometers through mountains without knowing what was happening in different areas. But today, within our territories, we can use drones and other technologies to monitor what is happening.

We can also train ourselves to ensure that we are using these technologies effectively. We can collect data to care for our territories. Today we can actually see where deforestation is occurring, which trees we are losing, what wildlife is disappearing in certain areas and what wildlife is returning. We can also monitor the quality of river water and measure changes over time.

These alternatives and tools help us create databases, strengthen monitoring systems and improve surveillance and follow-up.

However, this does not mean that every project needs to use these technologies. The important thing is that we now have better information about where the problems are and where we need to direct our efforts.

We also need to strengthen governance to help us reconnect with and relearn what elders have always transmitted to us. This is the only home we have. That is why we need to continue loving it, caring for it and protecting it.

New generations are increasingly influenced by Western systems, where the idea is that you only do work if you are paid. If you are not paid, then you may not continue doing it.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Olo Villalaz: An issue is that goals are measured differently, and perhaps for some organizations a project may not be considered a success, while for us it would be a complete success in another way.

Let me give you an example: medicinal plants. An organization supporting the planting of medicinal plants might measure success after one month or one semester. But for us, we need to look beyond that. We need to consider whether those medicinal plants will continue to exist, whether they will continue to heal different illnesses and whether future generations will still have access to them.

I believe that when projects are aligned with Indigenous ways of life, they can be a true success. But if projects are designed only from offices or from abroad, in ways that are disconnected from our realities, they will fail because organizations will not fully understand our ways of living.

Mongabay: What are the most common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

Olo Villalaz: Very few programs or projects have long-term financing. Most of them rely on short-term financing. For example, a project may be implemented for one year and everything goes well. But then the question is: What happens afterward? There are not enough long-term programs and projects.

Recently, I was part of a one-year project and communities were already asking, “What will we do in the second year if we are no longer receiving that support?” Many times, communities are left to assume these risks and figure out how to continue. Economically, they may have to invest their own resources or they may have to stop the work altogether. So short-term financing is a major problem.

Another issue is excessive bureaucracy. In previous years, we have worked hard to build trust with donors and organizations. We have invested a lot of effort into this because, from our perspective, many of the requirements being requested are not necessary or do not reflect the realities of our territories.

For example, if we are working with traditional knowledge, who should I turn to? An elder who has knowledge about medicinal plants. But what does the organization ask for? They say, “I need someone with a PhD or a master’s degree as proof of expertise.” That requirement is often at odds with our reality.

It is therefore important that organizations supporting us understand the realities of where projects are being implemented.

They also need more trust in the administrative capacities of Indigenous organizations. I believe there is still a lot of mistrust and a perception that Indigenous organizations cannot manage funds. However, in recent years in Mesoamerica, we have been working to demonstrate our capacities through activities such as supporting, monitoring, learning and collaborating.

Fortunately, we have gained more trust in this area. Almost all territories have created their own regional funds. These are territorial funds created by Indigenous peoples themselves to sustain their own capacities and capabilities.

There’s also a lack of collective decision-making in some projects. If projects are carried out by only two, three or four people, and only those individuals are responsible for protecting the territory, they will not have the same impact as when the whole community is involved. When we work collectively, our efforts go much further because we are thinking beyond ourselves and beyond the present moment.

João Victor Pankararu, youth coordinator for the Articulation of Indigenous Peoples and Organizations of the Northeast, Minas Gerais, and Espírito Santo (APOINME) (Pankararu land, Brazil)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

João Victor Pankararu: We have traditional practices related to water storage and protecting water resources, taking into account that our region has irregular rainy seasons, especially due to climate change.

In the northern part of Brazil, we have very important rivers. We have a river that connects two regions and crosses through our territory. The waterways that come into Indigenous areas are very well cared for to prevent them from being invaded or contaminated.

It is not possible to completely prohibit people from using water, but there are protections in place for certain areas where animals drink water (in order to protect people from becoming infected). There are reservoirs that communities can use for cleaning, as well as other areas that are exclusively reserved for drinking water. In addition, there are areas where water has a spiritual purpose. These areas should not be violated.

We also carry out reforestation activities by planting native species, especially in areas impacted by the presence of large enterprises nearby or drought. We choose to plant trees that grow quickly in order to support forest regeneration.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

João Victor Pankararu: Community initiatives, especially initiatives that involve the whole community and the different actors within the community.

However, when initiatives are implemented in isolation from the community, they are less likely to succeed because they often lead to a lack of engagement from the population. Activities that emerge from within the community are more effective because they mobilize more partners and bring more people together.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

João Victor Pankararu: There is a need to seek renewable energy solutions, for example. However, when these initiatives are implemented in our territories, they have too often caused damage. In my territory, for example, we have been heavily impacted by hydroelectric power plants and solar energy projects.

These are very large investments, and big electricity-generation projects have affected our lands. Around 90% of some areas have been privatized, with the land occupied by large electricity transmission towers that carry power to different regions.

At the same time, our communities are prevented from accessing quality electricity, and we do not even have access to drinking water in some areas. Sometimes communities cannot access certain water sources in the regions where they live.

These are very good initiatives in principle, as they were planned to generate renewable energy. However, they do not benefit communities, because some of these projects prevent Indigenous communities from accessing water and the infrastructure was built without properly consulting the communities. There was also no compensation provided to the communities living in the areas where these investments were implemented.

Mongabay: What are some other common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

João Victor Pankararu: There are many obstacles we face in Brazil. Brazil is one of the countries where there are significant attacks against Indigenous peoples who are fighting for Indigenous rights.

There are also government institutions in Brazil that have the mandate to oversee and regulate the recognition and delimitation of territories so we can govern the lands, but they are not fulfilling their responsibilities.

There are many business interests and industries along with people who directly influence the development of national policies that do not prioritize biodiversity protection. For example, there is the use of agrotoxins, as well as the exploitation of Indigenous lands, which weakens the management and protection of these territories.

I’ll share more. There’s a logic where, sometimes, people who design environmental projects do not fully understand the communities or the territories. Each community has its own particularities, which are very specific, and it is important for us to maintain this diversity.

There are different approaches that can be used to support different communities, allowing Indigenous peoples to determine for themselves the best ways to receive and implement support.

As Indigenous peoples, we have built our own Indigenous visions, which is different from the vision that was imposed during the colonial period, a period that attempted to portray Indigenous peoples as incapable or lacking skills.

We want to bring this into politics, advocacy, global engagement, academic knowledge production, communication, media, technology, management and leadership.

Abdi Akbar, director of political participation expansion at the Indigenous Peoples’ Alliance of the Archipelago or AMAN (South Sulawesi, Indonesia)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Abdi Akbar: The first is participatory mapping of Indigenous territories. This is not only about creating maps. It provides the foundation for protecting our Indigenous territories and establishing zones based on the customary laws that exist in our communities, for example rules to protect certain forests. AMAN is mapping lands across the country.

Another initiative with positive outcomes is the rehabilitation of Indigenous territories, especially in critically degraded areas. We carry out this work in areas that have been damaged by mining, large-scale plantations, such as oil palm plantations, extractive industries or natural disasters. We begin by planting native tree species that are best suited to the local ecosystem. Many native plants and tree species have become rare or are close to disappearing, so one of our priorities is to replant them.

Rehabilitation is also about using participatory maps to strengthen land-use zoning based on Indigenous laws and ensuring that these customary regulations are applied. Everything is connected.

In terms of zoning, we want to reestablish spatial planning within our territories. As our communities grow and populations change, our land-use needs also evolve.

However, rehabilitation must be connected to Indigenous knowledge. Before we restore the land physically, we first need to restore the way people think. The modern era and extractive economic systems have changed how many people view and interact with nature.

So, a key initiative is Indigenous schools. We established these schools to ensure that Indigenous values, traditions, knowledge and a relationship with nature are passed on from our elders to the next generation. In today’s modern era, many young people in our communities have access to formal education. While this is important, it has also changed the way some of them see the world, influencing their perspectives and mindsets. That is why Indigenous schools are so crucial.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Abdi Akbar: First, we need to ensure that Indigenous peoples and Indigenous organizations are strengthened. In both the Indonesian and global contexts, one of the most important solutions is to establish direct financing mechanisms that are led and implemented by Indigenous peoples. It strengthens Indigenous organizations, supports Indigenous leadership, improves the governance of Indigenous territories and reinforces our customary systems and regulations.

We also ensure the meaningful participation of women and youth throughout the process [of any conservation or climate solution]. The initiatives we find successful are led and decided by Indigenous peoples themselves, so the solutions are designed around local needs, traditional knowledge, and community priorities.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Abdi Akbar: In many cases, programs are designed without being aligned with the context, priorities and needs of Indigenous communities.

For example, there are carbon projects, carbon markets and carbon offsetting initiatives not based on Indigenous rights. There are also rigid conservation models that restrict Indigenous peoples’ access to their territories, as has occurred in national parks in Kalimantan [the Indonesian portion of Borneo]. For us as Indigenous peoples, we have always practiced conservation, even if we do not use that term. We have many different names for these practices in our languages and they are embedded in our customary governance systems.

When Indigenous peoples are no longer able to access territories because they have been designated as protected areas, this disconnects people from nature, even though that relationship had existed in harmony for generations.

Mongabay: What are the most common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

Abdi Akbar: Many externally designed solutions fail because they focus primarily on bureaucratic processes, economic interests and market-based approaches, rather than recognizing and respecting Indigenous rights. As a result, they are implemented through a top-down approach instead of being developed with Indigenous communities.

That approach basically ignores the reality on the ground, especially for Indigenous peoples. It also ignores the governance systems that Indigenous communities have already established. Decisions about programs and solutions are made by donors or project implementers, rather than by Indigenous peoples themselves.

I think that is one of the biggest reasons why so many of these solutions fail.

We also do not receive enough support or attention, particularly from our government. However, we continue to receive support from international organizations that recognize the importance of these initiatives.

We cannot do this alone. We need greater support and collective action. Working together will make these efforts more impactful and strengthen their contribution to climate solutions.

Sara Omi Casama, president of the Coordinator of Territorial Women Leaders of Mesoamerica, which serves under the Mesoamerican Alliance of Peoples and Forests (AMPB) (Ipetí Emberá, Panama)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Sara Omi Casama: I come from a territory where my grandparents were forcibly displaced by development projects while they were caring for and tending to their ancestral forests. Today, we find ourselves rebuilding as a community.

I say this to highlight our models of adaptation: Despite dispossession and despite violations of our rights, we have managed to reclaim the way of life of our grandparents.

We are healing a deep wound by continuing to restore our forests. When we talk about restoration, we are not only talking about planting trees; we are also talking about restoring our minds and our hearts.

There are positive examples within my community and across the Mesoamerican region that demonstrate what is possible. One of the things we have been advocating for is greater attention from academia and the scientific community toward Mesoamerica, because our region remains invisible in many ways.

We continue sharing knowledge and experiences: The factors that contribute to biodiversity conservation, climate adaptation and the strengthening of Indigenous territories.

Among the best practices I can highlight is the work carried out through the Mesoamerican Alliance of Peoples and Forests and through the Coordinating Committee of Mesoamerican Territorial Women. One important example is our funding mechanism, which is based on principles developed from the grassroots level and rooted in the governance structures of our territories.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Sara Omi Casama: Working hand in hand with communities while ensuring that our voices are represented. For example, every year, the Mesoamerican Territorial Fund also seeks to directly reach communities by working with their own governance bodies and with Indigenous women.

For me, these are examples that are moving in the right direction and that have the potential to be highly successful if they receive greater support. They also create opportunities for us to engage directly with decision-makers and move toward solutions that are grounded in the realities, needs, and visions of our communities.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Sara Omi Casama: There are still not enough mechanisms or tools that prioritize cultural relevance and that can truly create an impact within our territories.

Many programs and projects are carried out in the name of Indigenous peoples or in the name of protecting Mother Earth and claim to bring solutions to our territories in response to the impacts of climate change.

However, the majority of programs and projects are designed from above, from outside the territory, by people who do not understand the realities faced by our communities: the realities of women, elders, children and youth.

This is where conflicts emerge. Instead of seeking comprehensive solutions for our territories, these approaches often weaken the collective spirit and, above all, undermine the territorial vision and worldview of our communities. As a result, many of these programs and projects ultimately fail.

There are also projects that don’t guarantee our rights or that there is respect and that free, prior and informed consent from our communities is upheld in all decisions that affect us.

We also continue to raise the same concerns regarding Indigenous women, who are still being excluded from many opportunities.

Mongabay: Do you have any specific examples?

Sara Omi Casama: In Panama in 2015, there was a program called Techo de Esperanza [Roof of Hope]. The program focused on development and aimed to help families overcome poverty by providing housing solutions. However, it was a general national program that lacked cultural relevance. When it reached Indigenous territories, communities were essentially told, “Take it or leave it.”

Many families who needed housing accepted the option because it was something the government was offering, but the solutions implemented were not adapted to our realities. They overlooked proper sanitation, bathrooms and infrastructure that would ensure public health within our communities.

At the same time, these solutions disrupted the essence of our traditional homes. Our traditional houses are not simply physical structures; they represent education, learning, family relationships, community harmony and cultural identity. When those elements are removed, the result can actually create greater difficulties for families rather than improving their wellbeing.

These are examples of programs that negatively impact our territories because they often arrive without follow-up or evaluation. There are no processes to understand whether they are truly working or whether they are creating new challenges. They are simply introduced into the territory and communities are left to adapt as best they can.

Sometimes new interventions introduce elements that do not align with our worldview, without consultation and without seeking alternatives or mechanisms that would allow us to maintain our own structures.

Joseph Itongwa Mukumo, coordinator of the Network of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities for the Sustainable Management of Forest Ecosystems (REPALEF) and member of member of REPALEAC (North Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Joseph Itongwa Mukumo: One example is Kisimbosa, a community forest [in eastern DRC] managed by the Indigenous people of my own community in the Congo Basin. This forest is exceptionally rich in biodiversity and has been conserved by Indigenous peoples for generations. Today, it is legally recognized under the Community Forest Law. Communities have also established forest monitoring practices to guard against external threats and to raise awareness among young people about the importance of protecting these places.

Researchers from institutions such as the University of Kisangani have demonstrated the remarkable biodiversity found in Indigenous-managed territories, particularly with respect to fruit tree species, forest flora and the traditional management practices that ensure the sustainable stewardship of forests and biodiversity. Professor Raoul, a researcher specializing in forestry, demonstrated that the deforestation rate in our territory was approximately 0.3%, significantly lower than in neighboring areas occupied by other communities.

Similar examples can be found in the Kisimbosa forest reserve [in North Kivu] and in Kiri Territory, in Maï-Ndombe Province [western DRC], where an Indigenous-conserved area known as Koto once more demonstrates the effectiveness of Indigenous stewardship.

We have devoted considerable effort to documenting and bringing back to life our traditional practices that help maintain biodiversity, protect forests and rivers, conserve plant species and sustain wildlife. And, according to our customary rules, certain destructive practices are simply forbidden.

Our fishing practices also follow ecological cycles. During the rainy season, many fish migrate from large rivers into smaller streams. We know this is the appropriate time for collective fishing. Because we understand these migration patterns, we avoid clearing forests, cultivating fields or carrying out agricultural activities along the banks of these streams. Disturbing these habitats would damage the ecosystem and reduce fish populations in the future.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Joseph Itongwa Mukumo: To ensure these traditions continue, we pass our knowledge on to younger generations. We even maintain traditional schools where young people learn these teachings directly from their elders.

A priority is strengthening the capacity of Indigenous communities themselves, especially young people, who are the future guardians of our forests. Education, training and formal schooling are essential so that they can respond effectively to the external pressures affecting their territories. They need the knowledge and skills to understand national policies, engage in decision-making and defend their rights using the same language and legal tools as those who seek to exploit these lands.

The same is true for Indigenous leaders. Across our communities, local leaders need stronger capacities so they can advocate effectively for their peoples, understand the policy landscape and respond when their territories are threatened.

Our work focuses on solutions that come from within our own communities; not imported solutions, but solutions rooted in our values, traditions and the revitalization of our cultural practices.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Joseph Itongwa Mukumo: In 2022, the DRC adopted its law on the promotion and protection of the rights of Indigenous peoples, including the right to consultation before any decision is made regarding the use, exploitation or development of lands that Indigneous peoples have occupied and relied upon for generations.

However, this is not yet the reality. The implementing measures needed to enforce the law have still not been adopted, leaving many Indigenous territories vulnerable to exploitation without consent (free, prior and informed consent) or benefit-sharing despite the legal protections.

In response, one of our priorities has been to ensure that Indigenous-community-managed conservation areas are formally recognized within Indigenous territories, particularly where there is clear evidence that these lands maintain exceptional biodiversity and remain largely undisturbed.

To date, we have identified and mapped more than 40 Indigenous-community-conserved areas —our territories of life— covering approximately 700,000 to 800,000 hectares (1.7 million to almost 2 million acres].

We were able to influence this process at the national level and today community-managed conservation areas are officially reflected among the country’s national conservation objectives and contribution to the global 30×30 target, the commitment to conserve 30% of the world’s terrestrial and marine areas by 2030.

We have also begun advocating for the integration of community-managed conservation areas into forestry governance, both within the revised Forest Code and in related forestry legislation currently under review.

Mongabay: What are the most common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

Joseph Itongwa Mukumo: Among the challenges are the discrimination, marginalization and unequal status that Indigenous peoples continue to face. These realities mean that our traditional knowledge, cultural values and customary conservation practices are often not recognized by others as important contributions to biodiversity conservation.

Another challenge is the gradual loss of cultural values among Indigenous youth. Many young people grow up experiencing discrimination and seeing their culture devalued. As a result, some begin to underestimate the importance of their own traditions that sustain these ecosystems and believe that the values of others are more important.

Our territories also face growing external threats from things like logging, mining and armed conflict, especially in eastern DRC where there is intense competition over our natural resources. These pressures force Indigenous peoples from their ancestral lands. Indigenous peoples can only continue practicing and transmitting their traditional knowledge if they are able to live safely on their lands and benefit from the resources they protect.

Poverty is another major obstacle. When communities lack basic resources and are already living in conditions of hardship, they become more vulnerable to letting in external pressures.

Indigenous communities continue to face significant barriers in accessing the financial support needed to sustain and strengthen their conservation efforts.

Finally, one of the greatest challenges remains the lack of legal recognition for many Indigenous territories. Many ancestral lands we are protecting still have no secure legal status, leaving them vulnerable to encroachment and exploitation.

Toya Manchineri, general coordinator of the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon (COIAB) (Mamoadate, Brazil-Peru border)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Toya Manchineri: One of the key issues we are working on in the Brazilian Amazon for environmental preservation is the demarcation of Indigenous territories. Today we have more than 100 million hectares [247 million acres] of Indigenous territories.

These legal territories prevent the expansion of industrial agriculture, store carbon and help regulate temperatures, which is fundamental.

In Indigenous territories, we also have data showing that deforestation rates are very low in our lands. In some territories, deforestation accounts for only 1% to 2% of the total area.

Outside Indigenous territories, however, deforestation is much greater, particularly due to agricultural expansion and monoculture production, especially soy and other large-scale crops.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Toya Manchineri: Projects that create positive impacts are those that strengthen household economies while also strengthening community organization.

However, if a project is focused only on economic benefits, it will not produce positive results because communities also want to live well within their territories and maintain their ways of life.

We need to look at the territory, the land and the resources not as objects for trading or as things that can simply be translated into money.

The forest is a big village for many of us. We do not look at the forest as simply a forest, because it contains life, culture, plants, Indigenous knowledge and an understanding of how the world works. We need to look at life and spirituality so that we can heal our souls and take actions that truly contribute to the people who need support.

For example, if a family has $1 billion, where should those resources go? We need to learn how to share resources. We need to look back to the past and remember that there is a need to share with others.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Toya Manchineri: In the 1970s and 1980s, there were initiatives to plant coffee in Indigenous territories. Indigenous communities invested in coffee production, but many people did not have knowledge of how to cultivate coffee. These practices also reminded them of the history of slavery and, as a result, the projects did not succeed.

Another project organized by the Brazilian government was the hydroelectric power initiative, which divided communities who had different opinions and caused environmental pollution. Today, despite these impacts, the energy produced should be cheaper, but it’s not.

These examples show that projects that do not come from the community and do not involve the community in the process will never truly work.

Mongabay: What are the most common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

Toya Manchineri: Projects that are developed using a top-down approach may sometimes be received by communities as beneficial, but they are not based on the common practices or priorities of the communities themselves.

As an Indigenous movement, all the projects we carry out in Indigenous territories are implemented for and with the community. If a project is designed by the community, it will be more likely to succeed.

We should focus on what communities actually demand and prioritize activities based on those needs, so that they are not only sustainable but can also contribute to the economic stability of local communities.

Valéria Paye, executive director of the Podáali Fund (Brazil)

Mongabay: What solutions are currently working in your community, or in others, that don’t receive much attention?

Valéria Paye: There are collectives of people, such as forest guardians, who are restoring degraded lands and protecting important areas such as headwaters and regions that are essential for maintaining water systems.

These guardians also work on the protection and management of wildlife numbers. Indigenous peoples have traditional practices for managing species such as turtles, caimans and other animals. This is connected to our food systems because these animals are part of our biodiversity and food security.

There are also guardians who work to prevent and fight forest fires, which have increased in some parts of Brazil.

Even official data from IBAMA [Brazil’s environment authority] recognizes that Indigenous peoples are important allies in forest protection. We know that most fire brigades are made up of Indigenous people who are working within their territories to protect their own lands, as well as neighboring territories of other peoples.

Mongabay: What are some factors that make a particular conservation or climate solution more likely to succeed in your community, or in others?

Valéria Paye: Many conservation efforts require long-term political support and continuous state involvement. They need consistent support that can continue over time.

Our funding mechanisms at Podáali Fund can support initiatives for a specific period, but these broader efforts require longer-term support from governments and institutions.

I will also say: Solutions need to involve Indigenous peoples from the beginning and must be built from the realities of the people who are working in those territories. When solutions are brought by outsiders without consultation, they become increasingly inefficient.

Mongabay: What solutions are currently not working? Why do you think they are falling short?

Valéria Paye: These forest guardian and Indigenous fire brigade efforts have limitations, especially regarding access to support, equipment and protective materials.

The resources provided are often not permanent and this is something we hear directly from people working in these brigades.

For example, the government may establish a fire season and say, “We will support you from August to September.” But if fires occur outside of that period, communities often do not receive the necessary support. Some carry out these activities independently, outside the periods defined by the government.

This means there is a gap in protection at other critical times of the year. At Podáali Fund, we provide support, but we also face limitations because we can only support projects that have a defined beginning, middle and end. When those projects finish, our support also ends.

Mongabay: What are the most common pitfalls that prevent conservation or climate solutions from working?

Valéria Paye: I want to highlight something: complexity. For those of us from the Amazon where there are many borders, there are additional challenges. Indigenous peoples who protect territories, defend their lands and carry out this work are often the people who are most exposed to violence and criminalization.

We cannot talk about this without mentioning the threats related to borders, particularly drug trafficking. Drug trafficking is increasingly entering our territories, and these threats are directly affecting Indigenous peoples. The situation is getting worse. This is also weakening the work we are doing in our territories because we face direct confrontation with large organized criminal groups.

Our brothers and sisters are worried for their lives. They are witnessing new activities and new actors entering their territories, even luxury fishing tourism.

The state is not doing enough to monitor territories, enforce protections and address the threats that are occurring. As a result, responsibility has increasingly been transferred from governments to Indigenous peoples.

This bill would extend and expand several federal programs related to batteries, critical minerals, and advanced transportation technologies. What the bill would do

Reauthorizes federal programs focused on batteries and critical minerals.

Provides funding for research and development on:

critical minerals extraction and processing,

advanced vehicle technologies,

charging infrastructure and grid integration,

vehicle safety and mobility systems, and

electrification of heavy-duty vehicles.

Requires periodic reporting so Congress can track progress and program performance.

The bill includes phased authorization levels totaling about $2.9 billion for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. This money would support the federal programs, research efforts, and administrative functions created or extended by the bill.

Potential effects

If enacted, the bill would increase federal involvement in building domestic supply chains for critical minerals and in supporting technologies related to electric and advanced vehicles. It would also formalize planning and oversight requirements, including cybersecurity and workforce-related measures, for the funded programs.

text:
— -- The alternative-fuel revolution is driving prices of another energy-producing crop to near-record levels.

Soybean prices are expected to hit their second-highest average mark ever this year — and highest since 1983, says the Agriculture Department. Soybeans are used to make biodiesel fuel.

Production of biodiesel, a renewable alternative to diesel fuel, has increased more than 1,200% in the past three years, showing how the nation's truckers are being drawn into the alternative-fuels frenzy along with the auto industry. Last week, Imperium Renewables in Grays Harbor, Wash., opened what may become the nation's largest biodiesel plant. Production target: 100 million gallons a year. By locating the plant on the coast, the company hopes to be able to use plant oils from around the world, not just U.S. soybeans, says CEO Martin Tobias.

Other big plants are planned as well, moving production from 250 million gallons last year to an estimated 300 million this year, the National Biodiesel Board reports. Growth took off after Congress granted a production subsidy that took effect in 2005.

Renewable Energy Group, which bills itself as the nation's largest biofuel plant operator, runs six plants and has three more under construction.

Biodiesel is made from animal fat or vegetable oil. Although leftover french fry grease gets the most publicity as a source of the fuel, most biodiesel is made from soybeans. It can be burned pure or as a 20% blend in diesel fuel.

The rise in soybean prices mirrors a similar boost in corn prices. Corn is the primary feedstock in the USA for the gasoline-stretching additive ethanol.

Soybean prices are rising even though stockpiles of the oil derived from the beans are also at near-record levels, says Keith Menzie, an Agriculture Department economist. That's at least partly because the percentage of soybean oil production being turned into fuel is expected to be 12% for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, up from 8% last year and 2% the year before that.

text:
Solar panels on an electric vehicle are usually one of those features that actually turn out to be far less useful than they sound. The Deep Orange 17 project from Clemson University may change that perception. The team worked together with BMW to wrap more than 1,700 photovoltaic cells around a tiny electric coupe that looks like a homemade Cybertruck. According to them, the result is a car that gains more energy than it consumes during a typical day of city driving. But don’t get too excited — there are many nuances here.

What Is Luminetta and Who Is It For?

The prototype, developed by 16 graduate students together with BMW’s research team, is called Luminetta. The university says the car was designed for a daily commute of 12 miles (20 km). Of course, it is unclear how many people have exactly such a route, but it is obvious that it does not suit most. Nevertheless, the vehicle is designed to absorb sunlight both while parked and while driving.

Technical Solutions and Extreme Lightness

The main problem, of course, is that this is not an ordinary car at all. In metal, it is all solid flat angles and improvised panels. Deep Orange 17 weighs only 1,212 pounds (550 kg), about four times less than many production cars of similar size. Its multimaterial structure combines steel, aluminum, carbon fiber, and 3D-printed metal connectors. Regenerative braking, torque distribution, and optimized transmission control algorithms — everything is aimed at one goal: to use as little energy as possible.

Testing in Different Climatic Conditions

Together with partners from the Fraunhofer ISE Institute, Clemson researchers simulated solar radiation and weather conditions in four locations around the world: Greenville (South Carolina), Frankfurt (Germany), Madrid (Spain), and Mumbai (India). In these locations, according to the university, the solar system is capable of generating enough surplus electricity to add an average of 31 miles (50 km) of range each day. This is a groundbreaking achievement, despite all the caveats.

Of course, many other innovations will be needed to apply such technologies to a modern production car. But this prototype proves: it is technically possible to get more energy than is spent on very short… trips every day.

Photos: Clemson University / BMW

It is worth understanding that Deep Orange 17 is primarily a research platform, not a harbinger of an affordable production car. University projects of this kind exist to test bold ideas, and Luminetta does this job perfectly. The main lesson to be learned is that solar energy, even at the current level of technological development, can be not just decoration but a real power source for low-mobility vehicles. If such solutions are combined with more efficient photovoltaic cells, lighter materials, and smarter energy management, in the future we may see solar electric vehicles that truly do not need daily charging from the grid. Many obstacles will have to be overcome, but the first step has already been taken.

title: Africa wants more homegrown solar to boost self-reliance, but China's shadow remains
description:
