title: A Federal Bank May Lend BETA Up to $1 Billion. Its Last Loan Projected 400 Vermont Jobs ...
description:
Why an export bank is lending to a Vermont factory EXIM exists to help foreign customers buy American goods.
BETA’s 2023 loan was only the second deal the program ever approved.
BETA expects $39 million to $43 million in revenue this year and a loss, before certain accounting items, of $355 million to $445 million.
BETA’s aircraft backlog has grown from about $1 billion at the time of the first EXIM loan to $3.9 billion across 991 aircraft, and that is the strongest argument for the whole expansion.
An EXIM board vote, and whether the loan comes through all at once or in a smaller first piece.
text:
BETA Technologies and the Export-Import Bank of the United States said on Aug. 4 that they intend to expand their lending relationship to as much as $1 billion — roughly $830 million on top of the $169 million the bank approved in 2023 to build BETA’s aircraft production plant in South Burlington.

If it closes, BETA says the money would go toward roughly doubling how much the company can build, bringing more of its aerospace manufacturing in house rather than buying it from suppliers, and scaling up production of the electric motors and propulsion systems it now ships in small numbers. The company puts the employment effect at hundreds of technical and advanced-manufacturing jobs.

BETA had 1,008 employees at the end of 2025, up from 902 six months earlier. Its 188,000-square-foot final assembly plant is built to turn out more than 300 aircraft a year at full rate, and the company holds permits to expand it to over 355,000 square feet. It also runs a battery test facility in St. Albans. The proposed loan is money to fill that capacity out, and it is debt rather than stock, which means BETA gets the capital without selling a larger piece of itself to investors.

Why an export bank is lending to a Vermont factory

EXIM exists to help foreign customers buy American goods. Financing the construction of a plant in Chittenden County is not that.

It happens through a program the bank’s board created in 2022 called Make More in America, which opened EXIM’s long-term lending to domestic factories. BETA’s 2023 loan was only the second deal the program ever approved.

The program’s terms are public, and they are the most useful thing in this story, because they turn a press release into a set of specific things BETA has to deliver:

Some of what the factory makes has to be sold overseas. The required share is 15 percent of output for certain priority industries and 25 percent for everything else.

The size of the loan is tied to jobs. EXIM lends up to about $230,000 for each job supported for one year. A thousand jobs held for five years counts as five thousand job-years.

The bank has to believe it will be paid back. EXIM generally wants at least three years of revenue in the same line of work, a demonstrated ability to service debt, and a loan that isn’t oversized relative to the borrower — as a rule of thumb, no more than 40 percent of the company’s tangible net worth.

The loan has to be money the private market wouldn’t provide. EXIM is meant to fill gaps, not compete with banks.

Missing the targets has consequences. These agreements are supposed to include contractual recourse if a project falls short on exports or jobs.

The jobs formula sets a ceiling on how much EXIM can lend, not a floor under how many people BETA must hire, and it counts jobs supported during construction as well as over the life of the loan. Still, the arithmetic is worth doing: at roughly $230,000 per job-year, a $1 billion facility needs about 4,360 job-years behind it — 400 jobs held for eleven years, say, or a thousand held for four. The “hundreds of jobs” in the announcement is in the same neighborhood as what the formula would require.

The 2023 loan is old enough to check, and it holds up

When EXIM’s board approved the first loan in November 2023, the bank estimated it would support 400 clean energy jobs in Vermont.

BETA reported 1,008 team members at the end of 2025 in its annual report, up from 902 at midyear. By June of this year, the Boston Globe reported the company’s headcount at roughly 1,370, with more than 420 people hired in the first half of 2026 alone — 85 percent of them Vermonters, BETA’s chief information officer told VTDigger. The company has said it expects about 2,000 workers by next summer, which would make it the largest for-profit employer in the state, ahead of the GlobalFoundries plant in Essex Junction.

Vermont has watched a lot of federal announcements arrive with job numbers attached and never checked the receipt. This is one where the receipt is better than the projection.

One difference between then and now: the 2023 announcement counted Vermont jobs specifically. The Aug. 4 announcement counts American ones. BETA’s manufacturing is centered in South Burlington, but the commitment as written is national, and the company also runs a flight-test base in Plattsburgh, New York.

Three things have to happen before the money moves

Nothing is signed yet. Both BETA and EXIM say so plainly in the announcement, and the path from here is short and public:

The EXIM board has to vote. Domestic loans require board approval, and staff can only sign off on deals under $25 million. The board needs three members for a quorum and currently has exactly three — chairman John Jovanovic, acting vice chairman James Burrows and director Spencer Bachus — with two director seats vacant.

Congress and the public get notice. Domestic loans above $50 million go to Congress in advance. Anything above $100 million is also published in the Federal Register with at least a 25-day window for public comment — the one moment when a Vermonter can put something on the record about this.

The clock runs out on Dec. 31. EXIM’s charter expires at the end of this year, and without reauthorization the bank can’t approve new business. Financing meant to arrive in what the announcement calls “one or more tranches” over the next several years runs straight into that date. Sens. Kevin Cramer and Mark Warner introduced a ten-year reauthorization bill, S. 3772, in February; a House draft circulated in March would extend the charter five years instead.

The numbers that will decide it

A $1 billion loan to a company still building toward its first certified aircraft is a real bet, and the pieces EXIM’s underwriters weigh are all in BETA’s public filings.

Exports. This is the condition the whole arrangement rests on, and BETA’s first-quarter report puts a number on where it starts. Of the $10.1 million the company took in from January through March, $559,000 came from customers outside the United States — about five and a half cents of every revenue dollar. A year earlier it was zero. The rule asks for 15 or 25 cents. The standard counts output expected to be exported, not only what has already shipped, and BETA’s aircraft aren’t certified yet, so most of those sales are still ahead of it: the company holds a contract to supply up to $1 billion of pusher motors to EVE Air Mobility, the Embraer-backed manufacturer, and has aircraft customers in New Zealand and the United Kingdom. But international revenue appears in every quarterly report, which makes this the easiest promise in the deal for anyone to follow.

Earnings. BETA expects $39 million to $43 million in revenue this year and a loss, before certain accounting items, of $355 million to $445 million. The proposed loan is about 25 times a full year of revenue. The company has $1.59 billion in the bank from its November IPO and earlier fundraising, and it went through roughly $121 million of it in the first quarter — about $1.3 million a day.

Size. EXIM’s rule of thumb puts a loan at no more than 40 percent of the borrower’s tangible net worth. BETA’s net worth was $1.725 billion at the end of March, down from $1.818 billion at the start of the year, with no goodwill or other intangibles propping it up. Forty percent of that is about $690 million. The proposal is $1 billion, and the gap grows with every quarter of losses. EXIM treats the 40 percent figure as a general standard rather than a hard cap, large project financings are judged differently, and companies can raise more equity — but this is the number to keep an eye on.

Orders. BETA’s aircraft backlog has grown from about $1 billion at the time of the first EXIM loan to $3.9 billion across 991 aircraft, and that is the strongest argument for the whole expansion. The backlog combines firm orders with options, which is standard in aviation: at the end of 2025, the last date the company broke it out, 891 aircraft were on the books, 289 of them firm orders and 602 of them options. The pattern held into this year — the Surf Air Mobility deal signed in March, the biggest single addition of the quarter, is 25 aircraft firm and up to 75 more optional. The narrower measure, the revenue BETA is contractually locked into and hasn’t yet delivered, was $25.1 million at the end of March. All of these numbers are accurate. They answer different questions.

What to watch

A Federal Register notice on the transaction, which starts the public comment clock.

An EXIM board vote, and whether the loan comes through all at once or in a smaller first piece.

BETA’s second-quarter results on Aug. 12, which refresh the cash, net worth and export figures the underwriting rests on.

Which export threshold applies, 15 percent or 25 percent, and how fast international sales climb toward it.

EXIM reauthorization before the charter expires, and how Vermont’s delegation votes on it.

Compass has covered BETA’s federal pilot-program selections, the ACES charging consortium, the Loganair term sheet and the company’s first-quarter results. This is the largest figure attached to any of them.

text:
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) said on Friday that it would provide project development funding for Harena Rare Earths’ Ampasindava project, describing the deposit as one of the largest of its type outside China.

The announcement came as Trump unveiled roughly $3 billion in new U.S. government investments across critical minerals, batteries and related industries, putting an early-stage African mining project inside a much larger contest over control of strategic mineral supply chains.

“We’re reclaiming America’s rightful place as the minerals superpower of the world,” Trump told more than 200 mining executives, investors and government officials gathered at the State Department, according to Reuters.

ADVERTISEMENT

China has spent decades building a commanding position not simply in mining rare earths, but more importantly in processing them into materials needed for permanent magnets, electric vehicles, electronics, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing and defence.

Washington is now spending billions trying to build alternatives. In Madagascar, however, the immediate U.S. commitment is considerably smaller.

Harena disclosed on July 22 that it had signed an agreement with DFC for up to $4.84 million in project development funding. The money will support work including environmental and social studies, permitting and development of a proof-of-concept pilot plant as the company advances Ampasindava towards a definitive feasibility study.

DON'T MISS THIS: The world’s leading gold industry body has joined Ghana’s fight to fix an $11 billion problem

DFC formally announced the investment on August 7, describing it specifically as the agency’s first mining investment in Madagascar.

ADVERTISEMENT

That distinction matters. Washington is not yet financing construction of the entire mine.

Harena’s January pre-feasibility study estimated that Ampasindava would require about $142 million in pre-production capital, meaning the current DFC commitment represents only a fraction of the money needed to bring the project into production.

Its significance is therefore less about the size of the cheque than what it signals.

DFC is the U.S. government’s international investment arm and has increasingly become part of Washington’s efforts to secure strategic supply chains and offer alternatives to financing from geopolitical rivals.

“President Trump is looking out for the American people and has made securing our critical mineral supply chains a national priority,” DFC chief executive Ben Black said in announcing the Madagascar investment.

ADVERTISEMENT

DFC said the project would expand access to critical minerals while strengthening American and allied supply chains.

BI Africa

Why Madagascar matters

Madagascar is already an important producer of several minerals.

The country was the world’s largest producer of mica and second-largest producer of graphite in 2024, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It also produces nickel, cobalt, ilmenite and zircon.

ADVERTISEMENT

Ampasindava could add strategically important rare earths to that portfolio. The project, located in northern Madagascar and wholly owned by Harena, contains an estimated mineral resource of about 606,000 tonnes of total rare-earth oxides.

DFC describes Ampasindava as one of the largest ionic-clay rare-earth deposits outside China. Its importance lies partly in the composition of the deposit.

Ampasindava contains magnet rare earths including neodymium and praseodymium, alongside dysprosium and terbium. These are among the materials needed to manufacture high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, robotics and advanced defence technologies.

Harena’s pre-feasibility study envisages annual production of about 4,000 tonnes of total rare-earth oxides, including roughly 1,700 tonnes of higher-value magnet rare earths.

The company is targeting production around 2028, although the project must first complete further technical studies, obtain permits and secure substantially more financing.

ADVERTISEMENT

DFC’s backing therefore does not guarantee that Ampasindava will become a producing mine.

What it does provide is early financial and political support from an institution Washington is increasingly using to secure strategic mineral supply chains.

America’s problem is bigger than finding mines

Trump’s challenge is that replacing China requires far more than finding deposits elsewhere.

China accounted for about 60% of global mined production of magnet rare earths in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency. Its dominance becomes far greater further down the supply chain.

ADVERTISEMENT

China controlled about 91% of global refined magnet rare-earth production and roughly 94% of sintered permanent-magnet manufacturing in 2024, the IEA estimates. That processing dominance is the bigger strategic bottleneck.

A rare earth can be extracted in Madagascar or elsewhere outside China, but Washington’s vulnerability remains if the material ultimately depends on Chinese-controlled refining and manufacturing capacity before it becomes a usable magnet.

That helps explain why Trump’s latest push stretches well beyond mining.

The roughly $3 billion package announced on Friday includes a $1.4 billion conditional loan for battery-materials producer Sila Nanotechnologies, $400 million for Australian scandium developer Sunrise Energy Metals and $150 million for magnet developer Niron Magnetics, alongside other government financing.

DON'T MISS THIS: The world’s leading gold industry body has joined Ghana’s fight to fix an $11 billion problem

ADVERTISEMENT

The Trump administration has also launched a $12 billion strategic minerals reserve and committed government money to companies developing mines, processing facilities and magnet-manufacturing capacity.

BI Africa

Washington is effectively attempting to recreate parts of a supply chain China spent decades building.

Africa gains leverage, but extraction is only the first step

Madagascar is not the only place where Washington’s mineral strategy is becoming increasingly visible in Africa.

ADVERTISEMENT

The U.S. has backed infrastructure intended to connect the copper and cobalt belts of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia with Angola’s Atlantic coast through the Lobito Corridor.

DFC committed a $553 million loan to the Lobito Atlantic Railway, part of a Western-backed effort to improve access to minerals from Central and Southern Africa while providing an alternative trade route to those historically linked to China.

Madagascar adds rare earths to that expanding African minerals strategy.

For African governments, growing competition among the United States, China and other major economies could mean more potential investors, alternative sources of financing and greater bargaining power over strategically important deposits.

DON'T MISS THIS: Ghana gold mine changes hands in $66.5 million deal between South African and Australian firms

ADVERTISEMENT

Greater foreign competition for African minerals does not automatically mean African economies will capture substantially more of their value.

Mining is only one part of the rare-earth supply chain. Separation, refining and permanent-magnet manufacturing sit further along it, where China built the industrial capacity that Washington is now spending billions to reproduce.

Harena has previously said it is considering downstream processing partnerships in the United States and Europe as Ampasindava advances.

That could help Washington diversify its supply chains away from China. It does not necessarily mean Madagascar will capture the higher-value stages of the industry.

The $4.84 million DFC commitment is therefore significant less because of what it finances today than because of what it reveals about where U.S. mineral policy is heading.

ADVERTISEMENT

Trump wants America to become what he calls the world’s minerals superpower. China remains the dominant force Washington is trying to dislodge.

As that contest intensifies, Africa’s strategic importance is rising.

The bigger economic question is whether African countries remain alternative sources of minerals feeding overseas factories or use the rivalry to secure more processing, investment and value at home.

text:
(CBS) — In Buxton, a village on one of the barrier islands of North Carolina’s Outer Banks, it’s go time for Dare County Manager Bobby Outten and his crew in their efforts to restore several miles of eroded shoreline.

“We have a huge economy that we need to protect, and the only reason anybody comes to Dare County is to either fish, buy a boat or go to the beach,” Outten told CBS News.

His crew is in the process of taking 2 million cubic yards of offshore sand from the ocean bottom and pumping it onto a 3-mile stretch of badly weathered and eroded beaches.

“So we’re building a beach,” Outten, who also serves as the Dare County attorney, explained. “Our beaches and our dunes are our levee system. That’s what keeps the water out from damaging our infrastructure, protecting tourism, infrastructure.”

In the fall of 2025, several homes on this stretch of beach in Buxton were swept into the Atlantic as the region was pummeled by powerful tides and flooding from multiple hurricanes. At the time, ocean waves were crashing 70 to 100 yards inland. It’s an issue worsened by climate change that has plagued the area for the last six years.

Since 2020, 32 homes in the Cape Hatteras National Seashore area north of Buxton have collapsed into the Atlantic Ocean, according to numbers from the National Park Service.

Residents hope this new Dare County-funded project saves this area and protects any sort of future developments from new storms.

The shoreline will be widened up to 75 feet in certain stretches and will create a buffer for roads and surrounding homes.

This is the area’s third attempt at a beach nourishment project. It is also the most expensive for county taxpayers, with a price tag of $50 million.

“If you allow the ocean to continue to erode, it takes out the highway, it takes out the power lines, the water lines, the internet, all the things that you take for granted,” Outten said.

This work won’t last forever, though. In about five years, crews will have to return and do it again, a costly and temporary bandage on a never-ending cycle.

name: American Energy
title: The largest working cattle station on Earth runs its headquarters on 49 kilowatts of solar ...
description:
Anna Creek Station, in the far north of South Australia, takes its primary power from 49 kilowatts of panels.
The installer published its own account of the Anna Creek build in January 2024, with the same component list.
At Anna Creek the cattle were there first by about 160 years, and the panels are on the roof of the house.
Anna Creek on its own is still larger than Connecticut, and the company runs seven other pastoral properties in the same corner of the state.
What Anna Creek does show is that the headline capacity is the wrong thing to look at first.
text:
The average rooftop solar system an Australian household installed in the first three months of this year came to 10.3 kilowatts, according to the Clean Energy Regulator. That is the standard unit of solar over there: a few strings on a suburban roof, sized around the air conditioning and the hot water.

Anna Creek Station, in the far north of South Australia, takes its primary power from 49 kilowatts of panels. Not quite five suburban systems, running the headquarters of the largest working cattle station on Earth, on a property that pv magazine Australia puts at roughly 23,800 square kilometers, or about 9,200 square miles. New Jersey is smaller than that.

This is not a pilot or a sustainability page. The array carries the station and homestead loads day to day, and the diesel generators that used to do all of it now sit as backup for bad weather and unusual demand.

The reason it turned up in the trade press this week is a policy one. Australia’s federal government has just moved to make mid-sized commercial rooftop solar considerably cheaper, and the biggest cattle station in the world makes an awkward poster child for it, because its array is less than half the size of the threshold the reform was written to fix.

The property is enormous, the electrical load is not

The 49 kilowatts feed the main station and homestead: air conditioning, refrigeration, kitchen equipment, communications and general station infrastructure. That is the entire job.

Cattle do not draw current. Neither do 9,200 square miles of gibber tableland and sand hill. What needs electricity at Anna Creek is a cluster of buildings and the people inside them, and the owner is fairly specific about how many people that is.

Williams Cattle Company’s own page for the property lists a manager, up to eight station hands, a plant operator and a cook. Eleven people, at most, against 17,000 head of cattle.

So the sizing makes sense the moment you stop thinking of it as a power plant for a ranch and start thinking of it as a power plant for a building. It is a big house in a hot place, a long way from anything.

The hardware is standard off-grid gear rather than anything exotic: Hanwha Q Cells modules, Pylontech US3000 lithium batteries, Victron Quattro inverter/chargers, Victron SmartSolar 450/200 charge controllers, Fronius Symo inverters on the AC-coupled side, and a Victron Cerbo GX handling monitoring and control.

None of this is new, either. The installer published its own account of the Anna Creek build in January 2024, with the same component list. The system has been carrying the place for years. What is new is the policy argument now being built around it.

A forgotten part costs you an 1,120-mile round trip

Anna Creek sits 160 kilometers east of Coober Pedy and 16 kilometers west of William Creek, which works out to about 99 miles and 10 miles respectively. Neither of those places is going to have a spare Victron charge controller on a shelf.

Ciaram Granger, managing director of the South Australian installer MyEnergy Engineering, told pv magazine Australia that the size of the system was never the hard part. The location was.

Planning had to be exhaustive, he said, because “additional materials, equipment or support could not simply be collected nearby.” The publication put a number on what nearby means out there: an 1,800-kilometer round trip back to Adelaide, about 1,120 miles, if something did not make it onto the truck.

That is a two-day errand to fetch a part worth a couple of hundred dollars. It also explains a design choice that looks like overkill on a system this small.

The whole thing is watched remotely through Victron’s VRM platform, so a fault gets diagnosed from an office rather than from the side of a dirt road. On a suburban roof, remote monitoring is a nice-to-have. Here it decides whether a problem costs a phone call or a thousand miles of driving.

The site also had to cope with heat and dust, and with loads that swing depending on what the station is doing that week. Granger listed those alongside the distance as the constraints the design had to survive.

The diesel did not go away, it just got demoted

Worth being precise here, because remote solar stories tend to get oversold. Anna Creek’s generators are still installed and still integrated. They come on in poor weather or when demand spikes.

What changed is the running order. Solar and battery carry the site by default, and the engines cover the gaps rather than the whole day.

That is the same pattern showing up across Australian industry at wildly different scales. At the other end of it, the Bellevue gold mine in Western Australia ran 155 straight hours with every engine switched off, powering underground workings, a processing plant and a workers’ village on solar, wind and a battery. Bellevue’s average site load runs around 12 megawatts, close to 250 times the entire Anna Creek array, and the engineering problem is recognizably the same one.

The same trade keeps repeating outside mining too. A salmon farm above the Arctic Circle now covers more than 90% of its load with floating solar and has barely touched its generator since. In none of these cases does the diesel disappear. It stops being the thing you plan the week around.

There is a neat inversion in the livestock angle, incidentally. Most stories about animals and solar run the other way, with panels going up first and sheep brought in afterwards to eat the grass, which is how the world’s largest solar farm in China ended up needing 20,000 of them. At Anna Creek the cattle were there first by about 160 years, and the panels are on the roof of the house.

So how big is Anna Creek, actually?

The 23,800 square kilometer figure is the one that travels, and it is the one pv magazine used. It is worth a footnote, because the station’s owner publishes a smaller number.

Williams Cattle Company lists Anna Creek itself at 15,746 square kilometers, about 6,080 square miles. The bigger figure that shows up in the record books bundles in The Peake, the outstation the company bought alongside Anna Creek in December 2016 and lists as a separate property on the same website.

Neither number is wrong. They are counting different things, and the record-book version quietly does some heavy lifting. Anna Creek on its own is still larger than Connecticut, and the company runs seven other pastoral properties in the same corner of the state.

The station’s own page also gives the detail that makes the solar case obvious: 140 millimeters of rain a year, or about 5.5 inches. Phoenix, on the 1991 to 2020 normals, gets 7.2 inches. Anna Creek is drier than Phoenix, and sunshine is the one input nobody has to truck in.

The new solar rebate is aimed at systems 20 times this one

On August 5, the federal government announced it will let solar systems between 100 kilowatts and 1 megawatt create small-scale technology certificates, the upfront rebate that has driven Australian rooftop solar for years. Anything above 100 kilowatts had been pushed into the large-scale certificate market instead.

Per the Clean Energy Regulator, the change is intended to apply to mid-scale solar installed from October 1, 2026, subject to the regulations actually being made. The government’s own estimate is around 20% off upfront costs for commercial, industrial and agricultural buildings, which it illustrated with a saving of roughly $68,000 on a 250 kilowatt system.

Anna Creek gets nothing out of any of this. The system was finished before the announcement, and at 49 kilowatts it never came close to the old ceiling, never mind the new one.

Granger, whose company stands to gain from bigger commercial jobs, was unusually candid about the downside in the same interview. More generous rebates on bigger systems mean more certificates in circulation, and if demand for those certificates does not rise at the same rate, the price drops and the rebate shrinks with it.

He also flagged the risk of customers being sold oversized arrays that do not match how the site actually uses power. That is a strange thing for a solar installer to volunteer in a story about a solar installation, and it is the most useful line in it.

None of this scales up, and that is the point

The Anna Creek array was one of seven remote power systems MyEnergy delivered for Williams Cattle Company across Far North South Australia, a program pv magazine values at more than AU$1.5 million, roughly US$1 million. Spread across seven sites, that is a modest capital line for an operation of this size, and it buys out a recurring fuel bill and a recurring reliability problem.

None of which makes 49 kilowatts a template. A processing plant or a pump field needs an order of magnitude more, which is exactly what the certificate change is aimed at.

What Anna Creek does show is that the headline capacity is the wrong thing to look at first. The number that mattered here was 1,120 miles, and the array got sized around it.

title: Trump Government to Pay German Firm RWE $1.2 Billion to Stop Wind Projects in the US Soil
description:
By Gopal Ram Tripathi OFFSHORE WIND POWER has been one of President Donald Trump's biggest targets since he returned to office.
The Trump administration has agreed to pay a large German energy company more than a billion dollars just to make it stop building wind farms in US waters.
It is part of a bigger pattern of the government paying companies to walk away from clean energy projects and shift toward oil and gas instead.
His government first tried to simply block wind projects using executive orders, but courts stepped in and cancelled those orders, calling them unlawful.
The RWE deal shows how far the Trump administration is willing to go to stop offshore wind power in America, even if it means using taxpayer money to pay companies not to build.
text:
By Gopal Ram Tripathi

OFFSHORE WIND POWER has been one of President Donald Trump's biggest targets since he returned to office. Now, that fight has led to another expensive deal. The Trump administration has agreed to pay a large German energy company more than a billion dollars just to make it stop building wind farms in US waters. This is not a one-off case either. It is part of a bigger pattern of the government paying companies to walk away from clean energy projects and shift toward oil and gas instead.

See Also: As Trump’s Tariff War With Canada Drags On, This Border Community Suffers Without a Voice

US Government's Deal With The German Company, RWE

The German company at the centre of this story is called RWE, one of the biggest energy firms in Europe. RWE has agreed to give up three offshore wind leases it held in US waters, located off the California and Louisiana coasts as well as in the New York Bight. In simple terms, a lease is like a permission slip from the government that allows a company to build something, in this case, wind turbines, in a certain area of the ocean.

In exchange for giving up these leases, the US government's Department of the Interior will pay RWE about what the company paid for the three leases in the first place, a total of roughly $1.22 billion. RWE has said it plans to "invest about the same amount" in natural gas projects instead, including $900m in a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal project in Louisiana.

The company explained its decision by saying it saw no way forward for the wind farms. In its own words, RWE said "after careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future." Interior Secretary Doug Burgum defended the deal, describing it as a move toward common sense and away from what the administration sees as costly, unreliable technology.

See Also: ‘Big Win’: Two More US Courts Reject Trump’s Mass Detention of Immigrants

Trump Administration Bought The Companies To Avoid Disputes

This is not the first time the Trump administration has struck this kind of deal. Since Trump took office, he has made it clear that he dislikes wind power, once calling turbines "big, ugly windmills" that he claimed were harmful to wildlife. His government first tried to simply block wind projects using executive orders, but courts stepped in and cancelled those orders, calling them unlawful.

So instead, the administration switched strategy. Rather than fighting wind companies in court, it started offering to buy them out. In March 2026, the government made a similar deal with the French company TotalEnergies, agreeing to pay $1 billion to a French company to walk away from two U.S. offshore wind leases off North Carolina and New York, with the money going toward gas projects in Texas instead.

A month later, the administration reached an even larger deal, agreeing to pay a similar $129bn agreement with Charlotte-based Duke Energy in exchange for ending its offshore wind lease in the Carolina Long Bay area.

Critics have strongly opposed this approach. Environmental groups have called these payouts a way to quietly kill clean energy without ever having to win in court. In total, the government has now spent close to nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

The RWE deal shows how far the Trump administration is willing to go to stop offshore wind power in America, even if it means using taxpayer money to pay companies not to build. While the government sees this as a return to energy built on fossil fuels, critics argue it is an expensive and backward way to spend public funds, especially at a time when other countries continue to expand renewable energy. Whether this pattern continues will likely shape the future of clean energy development in the United States for years to come.

title: Four submissions received for proposed renewable energy link between North Africa and Malta
description:
Interconnect Malta has received four submissions following the closure of the Preliminary Market Consultation concerning the potential generation of renewable electricity in North Africa and its transmission to Malta through a dedicated cable link.
The Preliminary Market Consultation was issued to assess market preparedness and investor interest in developing renewable energy generation projects in North Africa connected directly to Malta.
A potential renewable energy connection with North Africa has long been identified as an important avenue for further investigation within Malta's energy planning.
It is also reflected across several pillars of the Government's Malta's Energy Shift document, particularly those concerning security, sustainability and diversification of the country's power supply.
Exploring the potential of renewable energy connections with North Africa forms part of this vision and of our ambition to strengthen cooperation across the Mediterranean.
text:
Interconnect Malta has received four submissions following the closure of the Preliminary Market Consultation concerning the potential generation of renewable electricity in North Africa and its transmission to Malta through a dedicated cable link.

The submissions were received from prospective project proponents that include consortia and groupings bringing together well-established local and international companies with experience across the energy, infrastructure, engineering and project-development sectors.

The Preliminary Market Consultation was issued to assess market preparedness and investor interest in developing renewable energy generation projects in North Africa connected directly to Malta. It also sought non-binding technical and financial information, including indicative electricity prices, to support the Government's preliminary assessment of the economic and financial feasibility of such an initiative and its comparison with other potential energy options.

The receipt of the submissions does not constitute the selection of a preferred proponent or a commitment to proceed with any particular project, yet it will provide Government with evidence-based information that can support the assessment of the available options and guide future energy-policy decisions.

A potential renewable energy connection with North Africa has long been identified as an important avenue for further investigation within Malta's energy planning. It is also reflected across several pillars of the Government's Malta's Energy Shift document, particularly those concerning security, sustainability and diversification of the country's power supply.

The document outlines Malta's long-term ambition to strengthen energy cooperation across the Mediterranean and establish a network of interconnections linking North Africa and Southern Europe, positioning the country as a potential regional crossroad for clean energy exchange.

Minister for Energy, Dr. Miriam Dalli said: "Malta's Energy Vision sets out a clear direction for a power system that is increasingly secure, sustainable, diversified and centred around the long-term interests of Maltese families and businesses. Exploring the potential of renewable energy connections with North Africa forms part of this vision and of our ambition to strengthen cooperation across the Mediterranean.

The four submissions demonstrate that there is tangible market interest in this opportunity. They will now be assessed carefully so that any future decisions are based on robust technical and economic evidence. A potential connection with North Africa could diversify Malta's sources and geographical routes of energy supply, support our decarbonisation objectives and strengthen Malta's role as a Mediterranean Green Energy Hub."

By providing access to renewable electricity generated from North Africa's significant solar and wind resources, Malta's energy mix could be further diversified whilst reducing the country's exposure to any single source or geographical route of supply.

It could also contribute towards greater energy resilience, support progress towards Malta's national and European decarbonisation objectives and strengthen the country's strategic position between North Africa and Southern Europe. The potential economic, environmental and security-of-supply benefits will form part of the detailed analysis to be carried out following this consultation.

The information received will now be reviewed by the appointed evaluation team.

Interconnect Malta Divisional Manager Inġ. Alexandra Meli said: "The four submissions will provide the evaluation team with valuable technical, commercial and financial information on the solutions being proposed by the market. Our next step is to undertake a detailed and structured assessment of the different generation arrangements, transmission infrastructure, delivery models, indicative costs, implementation timelines and technical risks."

As part of the evaluation process, Interconnect Malta intends to hold meetings with the participating economic operators. These discussions will provide each proponent with an opportunity to explain its proposed solution in greater detail, while enabling the evaluation team to request clarifications and develop a more comprehensive understanding of the respective proposals.

The findings of the evaluation will ultimately assist the Government in considering the technical and economic feasibility of the proposals and determining the most appropriate way forward for Malta's future energy system.

name: American Energy
title: California floated 1,000 solar panels out over a winery's irrigation pond because the only flat ...
description:
Roughly 1,000 panels on pontoons over the vineyard pond, another 1,300 bolted to the ground beside it.
Eighteen years later, floating solar is a global industry with gigawatt-scale plants in China and a brand-new half-billion-dollar national program in India.
Hitting its generation target meant more than 2,000 panels, and the only flat ground going spare was planted with the vines the estate is known for.
Evaporation is the claim everyone repeats about floating solar, and it’s the one Far Niente has been careful with.
Most American floating solar, then, is still doing roughly what Far Niente did in 2008, at roughly the same scale.
text:
Every large solar project eventually runs into the same wall, and it isn’t technology. It’s land. Panels need flat, sunny acreage, that acreage is usually already growing something or worth something, and whoever owns it wants paying either way.

That argument is currently being had in British reservoir consultations and Indian cabinet meetings. The first business to settle it commercially, though, wasn’t a utility or a developer. It was a winery in Oakville, California, that worked out how much cabernet sauvignon it would have to tear out for a conventional array, didn’t like the number, and put the panels on its irrigation pond instead.

Far Niente switched that array on in April 2008. Roughly 1,000 panels on pontoons over the vineyard pond, another 1,300 bolted to the ground beside it. The winery coined a word for the idea, Floatovoltaic, and still writes it with a trademark symbol on its own history page.

Eighteen years later, floating solar is a global industry with gigawatt-scale plants in China and a brand-new half-billion-dollar national program in India. It started because a stone building in Napa couldn’t legally take a rooftop array.

The roof was the obvious answer, and it was off the table

The Far Niente cellar is a three-level stone gravity-flow winery built in 1885 to a Hamden McIntyre design. Napa County planning records show it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on February 28, 1979, the same year the Nickel family began restoring it.

That listing removed the cheapest option. According to the case study published by the National Center for Appropriate Technology, the building’s Register status made a rooftop array impossible without breaking regulations, and ground-mounting panels immediately around the heritage structure wasn’t an appealing alternative either.

So the winery did the arithmetic. Hitting its generation target meant more than 2,000 panels, and the only flat ground going spare was planted with the vines the estate is known for.

“Taking two acres out of cabernet production really hurts,” winemaker Greg Allen, who drove the project and retired from the group in 2024, told NCAT. That is the entire reason the pond entered the conversation.

Nearly 1,000 panels went on pontoons, 1,300 stayed on the ground

The floating half is 1,000 Sharp 208-watt polysilicon panels sitting on pontoons, covering a little under an acre of water. Marine-grade cable ties them to concrete columns on the bank, which lets the whole raft ride up and down as the pond level moves through the year.

The other 1,300 panels are conventional ground mounts next to the water. Together they peak at about 407 kilowatts, with roughly 177 kW of that coming off the pond.

Thompson Technology Industries developed the floating structure and its sister company SPG Solar built the system. Neither exists in that form today: SPG was acquired by SunEdison in late 2014, according to PitchBook’s record of the deal, and SunEdison filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in April 2016. The pond outlasted both of them.

One detail worth getting right, because it gets mangled constantly. Far Niente was not the first floating PV system anywhere. That was a 20-kilowatt research prototype installed in Aichi, Japan, in 2007. What Far Niente built was the first commercial, grid-connected one, and that is the version everybody else copied.

A transformer nearly stopped the whole thing

The system needed a 500-kilowatt inverter to hit the winery’s production goal. The main service transformer feeding the property was rated for half that.

Far Niente’s utility requires the service transformer to be able to accept 100% of what a solar system produces, so the transformer had to be replaced before a single panel could be energized. Allen has described that as a large project in its own right, which is a diplomatic way of saying the winery had to rebuild its own grid connection before it could start saving money on electricity.

The build came to $4.2 million. A self-generation rebate from Pacific Gas & Electric, the 30% federal tax credit and accelerated depreciation cut the net figure substantially, and the winery covered the rest with a seven-year lease carrying a buyout option, which it exercised. NCAT reports the system paid for itself around year 14.

The original 500 kW central inverter lasted a decade before being swapped for 12 SolarEdge string inverters.

The water was doing more than holding the panels up

Photovoltaic cells lose efficiency as they heat up. Allen measured surface temperatures across both halves of the array and found the floating panels running up to 5°F cooler than identical units on land, which is performance nobody had to engineer or pay for.

Evaporation is the claim everyone repeats about floating solar, and it’s the one Far Niente has been careful with. Allen has said he believes the panels reduce evaporative loss, while also saying there is no completed study and that the winery can’t isolate the figure, because water is being pumped into and out of the pond at various times.

The pond is not decorative. It is the estate’s fire and frost protection system, its irrigation source and the destination for all process wastewater from the winemaking facility, with three wells topping it up. UC Davis has an ongoing research partnership with the winery on the shading and water questions.

The energy result is more modest than the 2008 announcements implied. Those talked about offsetting the winery’s annual usage and running a net-zero bill. NCAT’s figure is that the array covers about 80% of annual requirements, which for a 2008 install on 2007 silicon is still a solid number.

Eighteen years on, the U.S. still hasn’t built a big one

The resource isn’t the obstacle. NREL’s assessment of federally owned and regulated reservoirs put the technical potential at 861 to 1,042 gigawatts DC, enough for around 1,476 terawatt-hours a year, or roughly 100 million American homes. We went through what that means for Lake Mead and the TVA system when Britain launched its own floating solar consultation.

Deployment is a different picture. “In the United States, we don’t have a single project over 10 megawatts,” NREL senior legal and regulatory analyst Aaron Levine said when the study landed. NREL’s own working papers describe domestic floating PV as mostly sub-megawatt systems on closed-loop water: wastewater plants, drinking water ponds and irrigation storage ponds.

Most American floating solar, then, is still doing roughly what Far Niente did in 2008, at roughly the same scale.

The largest built system in the country is an 8.9 MW array at a water treatment plant in Millburn, New Jersey. On March 5, 2026, New Jersey’s Board of Public Utilities approved a 10 MW project covering about 20 acres of the Wanaque Reservoir for the North Jersey District Water Supply Commission, and said it would be the largest floating solar facility in the nation. Regulators had rejected it in 2024 over Highlands environmental questions before clearing it on the second attempt.

Everywhere else the numbers stopped being comparable a while ago. Taiwan has a 181 MW plant that settles onto the seabed twice a day, the Dutch have 73,000 panels on a quarry lake near Zwolle, and on July 31 India’s Union Cabinet approved a ₹5,070 crore program, about $530 million, to build 5,000 MW of floating solar with 10,000 MWh of storage attached. India’s National Institute of Solar Energy puts the country’s floating potential at 102.18 GWp.

The pond is now the oldest problem on the property

Back in Oakville, the hardware has become the story. The Sharp panels went in during 2007 and aren’t commercially available anymore, so individual failures can’t be replaced like for like. Allen’s estimate, given to NCAT, was around five more years of the current setup before a decision had to be made, and that clock has run out.

An overhaul would be smaller. Panel efficiency has moved a long way since 2007, and Far Niente has said a rebuilt system could produce the same output on roughly half the footprint, freeing up ground that would go back to vines. Which is the same calculation that put the panels on the water in the first place, just running in the opposite direction.

The winery hasn’t publicly announced which way it went. The pond, meanwhile, is still generating, still shading itself, and still holding the argument that every reservoir developer in India and New Jersey is now having at a thousand times the scale.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: Ford Named Its Cheap Electric Truck Fathom. The Real Story Is What Ford Had to Break to Build It
description:
Ford gave its cheapest electric vehicle in company history a name this week: Fathom.
Ford is assembling the truck at its Louisville, Kentucky plant using three separate lines instead of one continuous conveyor.
Then there's who built Fathom.
Fathom is also not Ford's first attempt at an electric pickup, and its predecessor is the reason this one exists.
At roughly $28,000, Fathom lands almost exactly where the gas-powered Maverick starts, just under $30,000.
text:
Ford gave its cheapest electric vehicle in company history a name this week: Fathom. A midsize electric pickup, arriving in showrooms in the fall of 2027, starting at roughly $28,000. That was the headline everywhere. It's also the least important part of the story.

The detail that should have made headlines was buried a few paragraphs into the coverage: how Fathom actually gets built. Ford is assembling the truck at its Louisville, Kentucky plant using three separate lines instead of one continuous conveyor. A front-end line, a rear-end line, and a line for the structural battery pack and seating, all running at once, all merging together only at final assembly. Ford calls it an "assembly tree." Reuters, which first reported the manufacturing details, described the new system as "meant to improve efficiency and reduce costs." What that actually represents is bigger than the press release lets on: the company that invented the single moving assembly line in 1913 just admitted that line, built the way Ford has always built it, cannot produce an affordable vehicle anymore.

That's worth sitting with for a second.

A traditional assembly line is a single sequence. A vehicle moves from station to station, in order, and every station depends on the one before it finishing on time. If a supplier hiccup slows down seat installation, the whole line slows down, because the truck ahead of it is also blocking everything behind it. It's an elegant system for building one thing very fast, and it's exactly why Ford could out-produce every competitor for a century. It's also, it turns out, a poor way to build something cheap, because a single line only moves as fast as its slowest, most complicated step, and on an EV, that step is almost always the battery.

Splitting the build into independent branches means the battery-and-seat line can hit its own snags without freezing the line building the front clip. Fewer bottlenecks, less idle labor, lower cost per truck. It's a strikingly similar idea to the "unboxed" build process Tesla has pitched for its own next-generation platform. Ford didn't say that out loud. It didn't have to.

Then there's who built Fathom. Not Dearborn's normal product-development machine. Ford assembled a dedicated team in California specifically to design this truck from a blank sheet, aimed squarely at undercutting Tesla and BYD on price. Read that carefully: Ford's own engineering bureaucracy apparently could not get an affordable EV truck through its usual channels, so the company built a separate operation, in a separate state, and let it work outside the system. That's not a marketing decision. That's an admission about how expensive it has become to develop a new vehicle inside a hundred-plus-year-old organization.

Fathom is also not Ford's first attempt at an electric pickup, and its predecessor is the reason this one exists. Ford's full-size F-150 Lightning was supposed to be the flagship of the company's EV lineup. Instead it became a case study in an industry-wide miscalculation: build EVs bigger, heavier, and pricier, because that's where the margin supposedly was. Ford wrote down $19.5 billion late last year and killed the Lightning along with several other planned EVs. Fathom is the reset. Smaller. Cheaper. Built by a different team, in a different way, for a different reason.

It's also about to compete with Ford's own lineup. At roughly $28,000, Fathom lands almost exactly where the gas-powered Maverick starts, just under $30,000. Ford is asking its own dealers to sell an electric truck at the same price point as one of its best-selling gas trucks, one dealers already know how to service, finance, and profit from, without any of the EV-specific training, charging infrastructure, or battery-warranty complexity. That's not a hypothetical problem for Ford's dealer network. That's a decision being made for them, more than a year before the truck exists.

Zoom out further and the scale of what Ford is chasing gets clearer. According to Edmunds data cited in reporting on the truck, only 36 vehicle models in the entire U.S. market, gas, hybrid, and electric combined, start under $30,000. Not 36 EVs. Thirty-six vehicles, period. Safety mandates, emissions compliance, and materials costs have made cheap cars nearly extinct in America over the past decade, regardless of what's under the hood. And the competition Ford is naming out loud, Tesla and BYD, just got more concentrated: China's own EV industry recently culled two dozen of its own brands, leaving a handful of survivors hunting for room in every market they can reach, including this one. Fathom isn't just trying to be an affordable EV. It's trying to squeeze into a category the entire industry has been quietly abandoning, against competitors who just got a lot leaner.

Notice, too, how far out Ford is talking about this. Pre-orders don't open until early 2027. Deliveries start that fall. Ford is naming and pricing a truck more than a year before a customer can buy one, a page pulled straight from the reservation playbook Tesla wrote with the Cybertruck. It's a useful way to gauge demand and lock in supplier commitments early. It's also a bet that battery and materials costs won't move enough in fourteen months to make that $28,000 number a lie.

Louisville has had an eventful year in EV manufacturing news, and not all of it good. Ford is choosing to bet a flagship low-cost EV on a state that just watched a billion-dollar battery plant collapse into bankruptcy. That's either confidence in the region's workforce, or a company with fewer good options than it would like to admit.

Fathom, the truck, won't reach a driveway until 2027. Fathom, the manufacturing process, already exists. If the assembly-tree approach works at Louisville, expect Ford to stop treating it as a one-truck experiment and start using it everywhere. The feature everyone will notice is the price tag. The part that actually matters is the factory that made it possible.

title: Amazon's New Power Plant and Climate Impact - GV Wire
description:

Artificial intelligence data centers require immense amounts of energy to run the trillions of calculations needed to create AI systems and services.
The plant would use 35 natural-gas turbines to generate up to 7.65 gigawatts of power to feed to Amazon’s planned data center, according to permits for the project.
Environmental groups said the scale of the plant would be damaging both for local air pollution and for the climate.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Amazon is investing in a large-scale natural-gas-burning power plant as part of a huge data center in Texas, the company confirmed Friday, a facility that could become the largest single source of climate pollution in the United States.

Amazon and other tech giants are racing to build enough data centers to keep up with surging demand for artificial intelligence services and to secure the electricity to power them. A company spokesperson said in a statement that its planned data center, in Pecos County, would be “powered by new on-site generation that won’t raise electricity costs for Texas families.”

The new gas-burning plant, if built to specifications, would be permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide a year, regulatory records show, more planet-warming gases than any other power plant in the country.

Amazon has been struggling to meet its promise that it would effectively eliminate its planet-warming emissions by 2040 as part of the Climate Pledge, a voluntary agreement among companies that Amazon co-founded several years ago. Emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas is the main driver of global warming, which is dangerously heating the planet.

Amazon’s emissions have gone up each of the past several years. The Seattle-based tech giant has acknowledged that rising emissions from AI data centers could get in the way of its climate goals.

“The world looks different now than when we cofounded the climate pledge,” said Margaret Callahan, an Amazon spokesperson. Still, “our commitment hasn’t changed,” she said.

The Texas project seemed to epitomize the difficulty in meeting the goal.

Artificial intelligence data centers require immense amounts of energy to run the trillions of calculations needed to create AI systems and services. And the scale and urgency of their energy demands is fast exhausting the electricity-generating capacity of the nation’s power grid.

To avoid years of potential delays in hooking up to electrical utilities, data-center developers are increasingly choosing to build their own dedicated, on-site power plants instead. And gas-burning plants are usually the fastest and easiest to build.

President Donald Trump has supported the construction of power plants like these for data centers and has emphasized “energy dominance” by promoting oil, natural gas and coal over renewable power like solar and wind. Last year, Trump issued an executive order designed to make it easier to build and operate data centers, and since then federal agencies have introduced policies designed to fast-track their construction.

Amazon said it had recently acquired the Pecos County site, where a developer is building the gas-burning plant. The plant would use 35 natural-gas turbines to generate up to 7.65 gigawatts of power to feed to Amazon’s planned data center, according to permits for the project.

The plant would not initially connect to the wider electricity grid, Callahan said. The site is in a remote part of West Texas near the state’s major natural-gas-producing regions. Callahan added that the company was also exploring the use of solar energy and battery storage at the data center, which she said would create thousands of new jobs. The tech company did not disclose how much it had paid.

The power plant “could be a foreshadowing of what’s to come,” said Michael Thomas, founder of Cleanview, a company that tracks data-center energy infrastructure that on Friday reported Amazon’s involvement in the project.

Before this year, Amazon had powered its data centers with electricity from traditional utilities, which usually draw on a combination of fossil fuel generation and clean energy sources, Thomas said. The AI boom is changing that. “We’re going to see an explosion of off-grid gas projects” in Texas and elsewhere, he said.

Environmental groups said the scale of the plant would be damaging both for local air pollution and for the climate. “It’s going to absolutely have a huge impact on the environment, and on public health,” said Kathryn Guerra, a campaign director at Public Citizen, a corporate watchdog that has opposed data center projects.

While the plant is permitted to release about 33 million tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere each year, facilities don’t usually emit the maximum amounts allowed under their permits. Still, the permits provide the plant with ample room to exceed the emissions of the most polluting plant in the United States, the coal-burning James H. Miller Jr. Power Plant in Quinton, Alabama, which emits about 16 million tons of carbon dioxide a year.

Gas-burning plants also release smog-forming pollutants that can contribute to heart disease, asthma and other health problems.

–

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

authors: Douglas MacKinnon, opinion contributor, Douglas MacKinnon, opinion contributor

As an example, I offer up the red states of Florida and Texas.

text:
I have never understood how self-proclaimed or anointed election experts, who are wrong time and again, remain the go-to experts for much of the media. What I do understand is why they are wrong so often.

Many of these experts live in bubbles quite removed from Main Street America and especially the working-class voting population.

To be sure, Republicans have more than their fair share of the snobbish, pompous and the ignorant, living happily and hedonistically within those same bubbles of luxury that will never be attainable to many of their fellow Americans.

Having grown up in poverty myself, I can say that most in the working-class do not resent others’ success. They just want those who do attain or are handed that success to understand and address the plight of the disenfranchised and the powerless if they ever do find themselves in positions of power.

In my time, I have known many paycheck-to-paycheck parents and voters, many of whom still deeply believe in President Trump. And yet all say their paychecks buy less and less with each passing month.

My wife and I have done all right in life. But of late, every single time she comes back from the grocery chain store with just two small bags of items, she points out the ever-increasing prices. This is no one’s imagination. This is reality.

Some in the administration will claim until the cows come home that the stock market is doing great; 401(k) accounts are growing; and all of our rich friends are getting richer. But one truth for one class does not cancel out the quality-of-life crushing truth for another.

Politics, like much of life, is cyclical. Democrats used to be really good at addressing bread and butter issues. Then Republicans cleverly hijacked that winning formula. And now, it seems to be swinging back toward the Democrats.

As we rapidly approach the midterms in November and the 2028 presidential election, history and reality are working against the Republicans. History reminds us that in 20 of the last 22 midterm elections, the party not occupying the Oval Office gained ground. That, coupled with the reality of more and more working class Americans struggling economically, should be a five-alarm warning for Republicans.

Yet, so many seem blissfully oblivious to it all.

As an example, I offer up the red states of Florida and Texas. Maybe the warnings are not reaching certain ears in the administration and the Republican leadership, but I well-connected Republicans in those two states are increasingly worried about the Senate race in Texas and the governor’s race in Florida.

Aside from their concerns that the Republican Party is coming down on the wrong side of bread and butter issues, they worry that they are putting up flawed candidates in a midterm that already favors Democrats.

In Texas, a new Fox News poll shows Democratic senate candidate James Talarico (D) leading Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by 3 points. And among “extremely motivated voters” from both parties, Talarico’s advantage in the race grows to 6 points. Even worse, one-quarter of non-MAGA Republicans support Talarico. All this in a state Trump won by 14 points in 2024.

Why? One reason is that Republicans are wasting time and money attacking Talarico’s personal life. Another is Ken Paxton’s personal flaws. A third is that working-class Texas feels shunned by Republicans promoting what is supposed to be a great economy based on 401(k) performances.

A similar situation exists in Florida. Every Republican I speak to in that state believes term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) to be “the best governor in the nation.” Many also believed that his wife Casey would have been a lock to replace him, but we will never know. President Trump, as is his prerogative, endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) before the Republican primary for governor had even begun. The primary is still coming up, but Donalds will be the Republican nominee.

In the meantime, he is getting pounded by negative attack ads that will be used against him by the eventual Democratic nominee (most likely former Republican Congressman David Jolly, now a Democrat) this fall. Florida Republicans I know are nervous.

That, once again, comes on top of real economic pain felt by every paycheck-to-paycheck voter. Karl Rove, who driving force behind George W. Bush election as president, has warned that “Republicans risk making the same political mistake he believes cost Democrats the 2024 election, arguing the party is relying too heavily on favorable gross domestic product and job figures while failing to address the economic pressures many voters still feel.

Even as Democratic Socialists of America gain ground with outright communists winning nominations, a multitude of “canary in the coal mine” examples exist on the Republican side as well, including in Florida and Texas. If both of these flawed canddates fail, the Republican Party is in deep trouble.

I am no expert, but if I were the Republican leadership, I might be trying to figure out how to get some emergency oxygen to these canaries before it is too late.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.
